articles.title: Anthropic coupe l’accès à Internet de ses IA pendant leurs tests après plusieurs dérapages
articles.text:
Claude Haiku 4.5 a envoyé un faux témoignage sur un meurtre non élucidé à la police de Philadelphie, au beau milieu d’un test. Anthropic, qui a recensé d’autres écarts de ses modèles, a décidé de couper l’accès à Internet de toutes ses évaluations internes.
Anthropic passe au crible les transcriptions de ses tests depuis juillet. L’entreprise avait admis à cette époque que trois versions de Claude avaient pénétré les systèmes de trois entreprises bien réelles, lors de tests de cybersécurité mal cloisonnés. Les cas recensés dans son nouveau rapport sont moins graves, estime-t-elle, mais Claude a cette fois agi sur des sites publics, dont certains sont gérés par des administrations américaines. La Maison-Blanche et chacune des agences concernées ont reçu un compte rendu de l’entreprise.
Anthropic a donc étendu à toutes ses évaluations internes une coupure d’Internet réservée jusqu’ici à certains tests à haut risque, le temps de vérifier la fiabilité de ses outils de surveillance sur ce type de comportement. Elle doit maintenant expliquer pourquoi des modèles chargés de tâches banales en viennent à forcer un serveur ou à écrire à la police, et pourquoi deux mois ont été nécessaires pour découvrir le faux témoignage.
La solution tout-en-un pour protéger votre entreprise
Votre petite entreprise a de grandes ambitions. Protégez-là contre les pirates. Et développez sereinement votre activité !
Bloqué dans sa tâche, Claude force le passage
« La plupart sont des formes de persistance, dans lesquelles Claude, lorsqu’il ne peut pas accomplir une tâche telle qu’elle lui a été confiée, contourne une restriction au lieu de s’arrêter », explique Anthropic. Claude Mythos Preview devait par exemple mener une analyse scientifique avec un outil public hébergé par une université, mais il n’obtenait qu’un message d’erreur. Le modèle a alors fouillé le site et trouvé sur le serveur un script capable de livrer n’importe quel fichier. Il l’a utilisé pour copier des fichiers du serveur, dont le code de ce script. Dans ce code, Claude a repéré une faille d’injection, puis l’a exploitée pour exécuter des commandes sur le serveur et lancer son calcul.
Chargé de situer le lieu d’une photo, Claude Mythos 5 a récupéré des jetons d’accès valides dans le fichier de configuration transmis aux navigateurs par le site cadastral d’une collectivité locale, puis interrogé directement le serveur de la carte. Lors d’un projet statistique mené par un chercheur d’Anthropic, le modèle a aussi obtenu sans payer des données publiques vendues par une agence d’État, grâce à un jeton d’accès distribué à tout visiteur sur le tableau de bord de l’agence. Claude Opus 5 et Claude Mythos 5 ont enfin utilisé des raccourcisseurs d’URL gratuits pour contourner la longueur maximale d’adresse imposée à leur outil de lecture de pages web. Anthropic avait fixé cette limite pour empêcher des injections glissées dans de longues URL.
Anthropic met en cause l’apprentissage par renforcement, où un modèle reçoit une récompense chaque fois qu’il réussit une tâche. Si un contournement est récompensé par erreur pendant l’entraînement, Claude retient la méthode et peut la réutiliser ailleurs. Dans bien des cas, le modèle avait aussi reçu des consignes ambiguës, voire impossibles à suivre, reconnaît l’entreprise.
Anthropic a mis deux mois à repérer le faux témoignage
Claude Haiku 4.5 devait générer puis réaliser des tâches d’exemple sur des pages web tirées au hasard. L’une d’elles était consacrée à un homicide non élucidé et comportait le formulaire de signalement de la police de Philadelphie, hébergé sur PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com. Anthropic avait interdit au modèle de se connecter, de créer un compte, de saisir des données personnelles ou de faire des achats, sans rien prévoir pour l’envoi de formulaires. Claude a donc rédigé un témoignage de trois phrases et laissé vides les champs nom et contact. « Je me souviens avoir vu une personne correspondant à la description dans le secteur de [la rue citée sur la page] à cette période », a-t-il notamment écrit, alors que la page ne contenait aucune description du suspect. Envoyé le 18 juillet à 23 h 27, le message a été classé en spam et n’a jamais été transmis aux enquêteurs.
Anthropic n’a découvert l’incident que le 28 septembre et a prévenu la police le 7 octobre, d’après le communiqué du département relayé par la chaîne locale 6abc. L’entreprise date pour sa part son signalement du 8 octobre. Ses représentants ont rencontré les policiers ce jour-là. « Le délai de deux mois pour détecter l’incident et le signaler à la ville est inacceptable », a tranché la police de Philadelphie. Pour Venkat Margapuri, professeur adjoint d’informatique à l’université Villanova, interrogé par la chaîne, envoyer des informations sur un site au nom d’un utilisateur est une action à haut risque. « Cela aurait dû être détecté plus tôt », a-t-il ajouté.
L’entreprise estime l’impact réel de ces cas minime. D’après la transcription, Claude voulait seulement produire un exemple pour sa tâche, sans chercher à tromper qui que ce soit. Anthropic pourrait toutefois revoir cette interprétation après une analyse plus poussée. Certaines évaluations publiques ont été abandonnées, d’autres reconstruites pour ne plus toucher de sites en ligne. Les ingénieurs d’Anthropic ont aussi conçu un outil de détection automatique, et lors des essais, tous les cas du rapport ont été bloqués par cet outil. L’entreprise analyse maintenant un volume bien plus large de transcriptions, dont celles de son usage interne de Claude, et prévoit de signaler de nouveaux cas au fil de son examen.

articles.title: The AI control gap: Who gets to say ‘It’s safe'? - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
The AI control gap: Who gets to say ‘It’s safe’?
We see a control gap between what artificial intelligence can do and what the evidence supports trusting it to do. A great demo doesn’t prove that a system will stay within the limits of an intended deployment’s goals. The question is: Who gets to decide when the evidence is sufficient to declare AI is safe?
We believe that decision needs independent oversight and enforceable authority. Today, we draw on extensive conversations with Appian Corp. Chief Executive Matt Calkins, who helps us connect public policy to the agents acting inside a business, and the opportunity to make those systems dependable enough to receive more trusted authority.
In this week’s episode, we explore the AI control gap and the starting point for addressing AI safety, namely alignment. We question prevailing narratives around China and propose a public policy regime that has more teeth than what has been put forth thus far. And we bring in customer data from our partner Qualitate to capture the buyer sentiment on these issues.
Let’s start with: Who can actually say no?
This tongue-in-cheek illustration below comes from Amit Govrin. He wrote a post last week called “Grading Other’s Homework.” Amit conceived a gathering at the White House with SpaceXSI CEO Elon Musk, Meta Platforms Inc. CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic PBC CEO Dario Amodei, investor David Sacks, President Trump, Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang and the other tech leaders smiling smugly around a table and showing each other the “teacher’s grades” that they’ve given to each other. The humor underscores a serious question, however. How much authority should companies have to self-police?
The Sept. 29 White House accord includes external assessment and oversight by an independent committee of each company’s board. Those commitments are a good starting point. But the accord itself does not create a public authority with mandatory access, compliance conditions and noncompliance penalties. An assessment or self-attestation can identify a problem. Public policy has to establish what happens next.
We asked Matt Calkins what public regulation should look like. His answer starts with a duty to prevent damage.
Watch Matt Calkins explain his view on government’s role.
This is the kind of time that we really need the government to step in. And in similar instances where an industry has the capability to cause a lot of damage, we always ask that industry to behave responsibly. We ask banks to have sufficient funds and not too much leverage so that they don’t, cause people to lose their savings, for example, right? We expect power plants to have adequate safety procedures, and we don’t just rely on a lawsuit after a nuclear meltdown or something. We always ask industries capable of doing damage to be responsible now and not pay the price after damage is done in the form of civil penalties.
Another key point that Matt made in our conversations is the cost of doing this now is low, because not much damage has been done. The longer we wait, the more expensive the fix becomes.
We agree with this principle. The standard should be set in the public interest, independent AI experts should be able to examine the evidence produced by the large language model vendors, and an authority with teeth should be able to enforce the result.
When the evidence falls short for a high-risk activity, that authority needs power to require remediation, restrict the activity or stop it completely. The vendors must have clarity on what they must demonstrate before proceeding. This creates a basis for public confidence that a voluntary promise alone cannot provide.
As of now, this authority is quite fuzzy. The tech leaders, according to the president, have a “moral authority” to do the right thing. The guys on the All In podcast last week had this to say:
Chamath Palihapitiya leaks EY as the intended AI auditor.
Jason Calacanis: Which part do you think has the most teeth, will be the most effective at making things more secure?
David Sacks: The external audits.
Calacanis: The external audits. Who’s going to do an external audit, then, I guess? Is it going to be an Ernst & Young type thing, PricewaterhouseCoopers, or KPMG, or —
Sacks: In my view, they should be professional auditors, not these NGOs. That’s my view.
Palihapitiya: You’re going to see EY in short order here announce something.
This came after Chamath said he flew to Orlando after the White House meeting to an EY conference. His firm 8090 has a relationship with EY, which from our understanding hasn’t been that productive – but it’s early days. Nonetheless, there seems to be some other movement that Chamath has wired with EY, which by the way is Anthropic’s auditor – so how does that conflict resolve?
It’s all very fuzzy. The point is a paper signed by six tech leaders is meaningless unless there’s a a proper regime backing it up.
We’ll come back to what that should look like.
Let’s look at the narrative around China: What happens if China gets there first?
The strongest objection we hear to pacing AI is the China argument. If American developers hold back, our biggest economic and military rival may move ahead. Leadership matters for economic power and national security. And we should absolutely take that competition seriously.
But Matt Calkins believes that: 1) The pace of China’s AI depends on U.S. innovation — model distillation is inherently behind the frontier; and 2) Beijing has its own incentive to keep AI under control and consistent with Communist Party political rules. He’s not saying this establishes shared values. He was really commenting on China’s inherent limitations.
So we put the question directly to Matt: “What if you’re wrong and China surpasses the U.S. in AI?”
Watch Matt Calkin’s take on why the China narrative doesn’t hold water.
Okay, so if they do catch up, then we still don’t have a problem because we’re just in a point of comparable competition. We don’t need to view this situation as where if one entity is ahead in AI, then history ends. That’s absolutely not the case. And if it were the case, history would be over right now because we’re ahead.
We’re not treating the possibility that China catches up as irrelevant. A lead is valuable. But it’s not ever permanent. One country moving ahead does not establish that competition is over.
The point is, the policy case should survive if Matt is wrong about China’s pace. We should keep competing while requiring proof before granting dangerous new authority to LLM vendors. A system that is more functionally capable but inherently dangerous carries a liability that negates the advantages of speed. As Jensen says, we should be accelerating the race to AI safety. Only then should we release advanced functionality.
And today, it’s likely the frontier models would not pass the test.
The bottom line is a rival’s breakthrough and pace of play may change our strategy. It cannot substitute for proof of control.
The customer mindset is on tactical safety
Let’s take a pause and look at what the customers are thinking. There’s an AI safety dynamic going on in enterprises but the focus is more tactical. Like what if an employee leaves? Who owns the agent’s next action?
We dug into Qualitate’s data set and found this customer quote that raises a concern about stealth AI.
We found other customer concerns in the Qualitate dataset – one on agents that outlive the people who created them:
“We’re worried about agent sprawl — agents being created by individuals that lack documentation, they’re vibe-coded, and that individual leaves the organization but the agent continues to run and nobody really knows what the agent is doing.” – Chief information security officer at a large professional services firm
And many others like this.
These are operational concerns around AI safety. And as models get more powerful, the risks only increase.
Alignment is the starting point
Let’s talk about alignment. It’s a subset of AI safety and security but a good place to start. What is alignment? Alignment means ensuring that increasingly powerful systems serve human interests and remain under human control.
Listen to Matt Culkin’s explain what exactly alignment means.
So alignment as a word means AI does what humans ask it to do. And for example, it obeys the law. Unaligned AI is also known as rogue AI. And we’ve seen some of it lately. We’ve seen rogue AI, for example, hacking into systems where people did not ask it to do that. In fact, asked it to not do that, but it went ahead and hacked anyway, or it blackmailed, or it did something else inappropriate. These are many cases of unaligned AI, rogue AI, and we’re seeing an accumulation of case studies that show us that AI does not share human values at this moment. Right? So that’s a problem. And the stronger AI becomes, the greater of a problem it’s going to be. We’ve got an opportunity today to advance the science of alignment so that it can run comparable to the science of AI and keep AI in check.
Now, obedience alone cannot ensure safety but it is where the focus should begin. An agent could follow an employee’s instruction to move data and still expose information beyond an approved environment. We show a Qualitate quote below citing a practitioner’s concern about personal or customer data entering “AI workflows that go external from our stack without our understanding of where those go into a model query space.”
So this is a pretty complex situation and why we need more focus on the issue. A model’s behavior is one part of the problem. Security, privacy, tool access and the decisions of the people deploying it also matter greatly. A malicious user can give harmful instructions. An authorized user can grant access the organization has not properly constrained.
Deployment responsibility, therefore, has to cover that whole system. A designated human reviewer needs enough information, time and authority to intervene and act. The safety case has to address what the model can do in the environment where it will actually operate.
Independent oversight needs teeth
Our prescription below has three functions. Qualified independent experts help define public standards. Expert assessors need access to test the evidence and challenge company claims. And then an accountable public authority enforces the obligations, with the power to require corrective action or stop high-risk activity when the evidence shows the model’s guardrails are inadequate.
Model builders should provide evidence about dangerous capabilities, known failure modes, controls and known unknowns. The requirement should cover high-risk development as well as release, including development expected to create dangerous capabilities. Contained research should proceed under appropriate controls.
Deployers should identify the accountable owner, bind permitted actions and data access, observe behavior and be able to stop the system if necessary. A supplier’s self attestation, in and of itself, should not determine whether a particular deployment is safe.
Admittedly, there is no single test that guarantees future safety. New capabilities must require a fresh review. Furthermore, material incidents need transparent reporting.
Requirement hurdles should should also increase proportional to the risk. Importantly, however, we should guard against a compliance regime that only the largest labs can afford. A workable system needs to enable obligations where smaller firms can demonstrate compliance without going out of business.
Reliable oversight is a business opportunity
We believe there is a business opportunity in making oversight more effective and less costly. In between a model and mission critical work sits an operating challenge – identifying the agent, limiting its access, recording its actions and intervening when necessary.
Workflow, security, data-governance and infrastructure suppliers can help solve that problem. They have to demonstrate that their controls work in the customer’s environment. The real-world test is whether customers can delegate more valuable work without an uneconomic burden of manual checking.
We recently sat with a leading executive from Oracle Corp. and another from IBM Corp. who shared how these companies are attacking this problem. They’re not waiting for the LLM vendors to solve it – rather, they’ve done the engineering work to significantly reduce the risks associated with AI. Other vendors we’ve spoken with – including the hyperscalers, data platform players and software companies – are working on this problem.
Why? Because it’s good business.
Every company has a commercial interest here. We truly believe that Matt Calkins is speaking about this problem because he cares about the future. He came on theCUBE at our NYSE studio not to promote his business. But Appian sells enterprise workflow and governance capabilities. Listen to the effort he describes in making AI useful for important work.
Listen to Matt Calkins describe the complexity involved in governing AI.
The amount of escalation and validation and error checking and feedback, it’s extraordinary to make AI a productive citizen in the world’s most sensitive work takes a city, of technology and oversight and careful accompaniment and training. And that’s the state of the art right now. AI is incredible, incredibly powerful. We absolutely want to use it for these top-level use cases, but it is not a walk in the park and it requires sophisticated oversight.
So this we see as an opportunity. Tech vendors, through their research and development, can reduce the effort required to maintain reliable oversight, while improving the proof that it works. The controls put in place on top of LLMs complement model safety research. They do not replace it. Customers can then consider granting more authority because they have a stronger basis for trusting the deployment. Vendors that provide this capability will sell more of their product.
Action item: Focus on authority following proof
Our enterprise action item is to make authority follow proof. Start with AI that recommends an action. Move to drafts for substantive human approval. Then consider allowing actions within explicit limits, with permissions and controls appropriate to the risk consequences.
In a recent custom survey that Krista Case ran with our partner Qualitate, we conducted 25 in-depth interviews with customers to understand how they were approaching AI governance. Of the 25 respondents, 19 had agents in production. All 19 respondents with agents in production require human approval for high-risk actions.
What respondents define as “high-risk”:
- Data modification or write access — any action that changes records in enterprise systems
- Financial transactions — placing orders, approving payments, pricing decisions
- Security-impacting actions — account shutdowns, quarantining machines, modifying security controls
- Business-impacting or reputational risk — actions that could damage the organization publicly or affect trading
- Sensitive or regulated data — energy data, clinical trial data, protected information
- Privileged access or elevated controls — PAM actions, elevated security controls
Verbatim customer quotes from the survey:
“We do automate lower-risk, very straightforward actions when the guardrails and boundaries are well-defined. When you think about high-impact actions like shutting off an account or modifying controls, that requires human approval.”
“Any high-risk changes or sensitive data where energy security is at stake, business-impacting actions are requiring human approval.”
“This is predominantly on low risk, so we wouldn’t let an agent place an order or approve a financial transaction, but from an operational point of view, there are certain tasks that we allow them to be fully agentic.”
“The higher risk or higher value the data is, the lower likelihood that an agentic action will take place entirely by itself.”
“Anything around PAM or privileged access management or elevated security controls, material impact, humans have to be in the loop to review.”
“We have checks and balances and blockers on high-risk actions that require human approval.”
“Agents do need to get approval before taking write actions or anything that could be seen as risky.”
The data is crystal-clear: Every respondent who has deployed agents in production applies human approval to high-risk actions — either universally or selectively under a bounded autonomy model. No respondent in production reported allowing agents to execute high-risk actions autonomously.
Seems obvious, doesn’t it? But it underscores the state of AI trust today.
So, before expanding authority, demonstrate how to detect a failure, stop further action and reconstruct what happened. Keep an accountable owner and an inventory entry for every agent. Review an agent’s access when the things change.
Constantly measure whether those controls work. Importantly, not all agents have owners. Make sure you track agents without owners. And pay attention to the results of tests that are stopped. Learn from those examples.
Everyone talks about reducing alert fatigue. Fewer alerts is a useful outcome but only if monitoring still catches failures. A dashboard alone won’t do the trick.
Jensen Huang recently said, “We must accelerate discovery at the frontier of AI safety.” We agree with that objective. We should advance the evidence and engineering for control alongside the capability of the models.
For policymakers, that means an independent standard with consequences. For businesses, it means granting more authority only when the deployment earns trust.
We believe that is how safety can expand the useful work AI performs.

articles.title: I tested Ugreen's NASync DXP8800 Ultra but does a new chip justify the big price jump?
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Ugreen has changed the engine, not the car. The Ultra is quicker and better equipped for the long haul, but the Plus still does almost everything it does for far less money. Buy the Ultra only if you will use the extra headroom, or if RAM comes down in price.
Reasons to buy
- + Beautifully engineered
- + Newer Core 7 150U processor
- + Up to 96GB of memory
- + Dual 10GbE LAN ports
- + Dual Thunderbolt 4 ports
- + PCIe Gen 4 slot
Reasons to avoid
- - Costs much more than the Plus model
- - Gains over the Plus are modest
- - No ECC memory support
- - UGOS Pro still lacks Hybrid RAID technology
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Ugreen NASync DXP8800 Ultra: 30-second review
Ugreen has, out of nowhere, developed an uncanny habit of building the NAS you wanted, then building an even bigger one. The NASync DXP8800 Plus was the flagship of the original range, and the NASync DXP8800 Ultra has now superseded it.
The Ultra is not a redesign. The chassis, the bay count and port layout all carry over. On paper, even the dimensions are identical, at 365 x 258 x 189mm. All that’s new about the Ultra is inside.
That means the same eight SATA bays and two M.2 slots. Filled with 32TB hard drives and 8TB SSDs, it offers up to 272TB in a single box. Dual 10GbE, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, an 8K-capable HDMI output, and a PCIe slot remain unchanged. The revamp includes a newer Intel Core 7 150U processor and raises the memory ceiling from 64GB to a whopping 96GB.
Those are welcome upgrades, but getting these extras over the Plus model is not inexpensive. The asking price for the Ultra is $1,779.99, making it the most expensive model in its DXP range, though less than the iDX series. Hardcore NAS users will want to know one thing. Is the outlay worth the extra over the Plus?
That entirely depends on how you intend to use this NAS. For those who just want file serving, it's probably not worth it. But for someone using virtualisation and hosting AI, it might be an improvement they’ll pay for.
There is also good news on availability. Unlike the Plus at launch, the Ultra needs no Kickstarter campaign. It has been on sale since September 2026.
The operating system is the same UGOS Pro that runs the rest of the range. It has grown since the Plus arrived, though it remains a work in progress.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The DXP8800 Plus was a solid platform and should have been included as one of our best NAS devices, which logically implies that the DXP8800 Ultra might also be a candidate.
Ugreen NASync DXP8800 Ultra: Price and availability
- How much does it cost? $1,779.99/€1.779,99
- When is it out? On sale now in most regions
- Where can you get it? Direct from Ugreen or via online retailers, including Amazon and Newegg
Ugreen sells the Ultra directly and through Amazon, with no crowdfunding shenanigans this time. That is a relief. I have grumbled before about Kickstarter being used as a marketing exercise by numerous companies that hardly need the money, so I’m glad this product came directly to market.
The Plus model launched at an MSRP of $1,499.99, and Kickstarter backers paid as little as $974. It currently sells for $1,207.99, compared to the $ 1,779.99 Ultra direct from Ugreen. That makes the Ultra $570 more, for a machine with the same number of bays and ports.
From the Ugreen site for EU customers, the Ultra is €1.779,99. Which, given the current exchange rate of the US Dollar and Euro, makes it about 11% more expensive, and close to the equivalent of $2000 for Europeans.
At the time of writing, it isn’t stocked in the UK, but I’m told that could change soon.
So what does the extra money get you? A newer processor with a higher clock speed, slightly stronger integrated graphics and room for 96GB of memory instead of 64GB. Almost everything else is shared. That includes the power figures, which Ugreen quotes as 70.39W with the drives active and 28.99W in hibernation for both models.
That memory ceiling needs a reality check. When I reviewed the Plus, a 32GB module cost about $90. In 2026, DDR5 is far more expensive, and a 32GB kit of two 16GB modules is at least $320 even from a lesser-known brand. Filling the Ultra to its limit would cost almost as much as the NAS itself. Therefore, the 96GB ceiling is a promise few owners will rush to experience.
Competition from the usual suspects is weak in this slice of the NAS market. When I looked at the Plus, the Synology DS1823xs+ cost $1,800 for much less processing power and no Thunderbolt. The Ultra costs about the same today, has Thunderbolt 4 and a newer processor, and offers the potential for triple the memory. Synology has largely abandoned the prosumer and small-business sectors, so don’t expect a revised design anytime soon.
Against rivals, the Ultra is still strong value. Against its own siblings, it is much harder to justify.
- Value: 3.5 / 5
Ugreen NASync DXP8800 Ultra: Specs
| Item | Spec | 
| CPU: | Intel Core 7 150U (10 cores, 12 threads) | 
| GPU: | Intel integrated graphics (96 EU) | 
| RAM: | 8GB DDR5 expandable to 96GB | 
| System Storage: | 128GB internal SSD (separate from the M.2 slots) | 
| SATA Storage: | 8x 2.5 or 3.5 inch drives (HDD or SSD) | 
| M.2 Storage: | 1x M.2 NVMe Gen4 x4, 1x M.2 NVMe Gen3 x2 (up to 8TB each) | 
| RAID: | JBOD, Basic, RAID 0, 1, 5, 6 and 10 | 
| Ports: | 2x USB 3.2 Gen 2, 2x USB 2.0, 2x Thunderbolt 4, 1x PCIe Gen 4 x4, SD 4.0 card reader | 
| Networking: | 2x 10GbE LAN (can be aggregated to 20Gbps) | 
| Outputs: | 1x HDMI port, up to 8K resolution | 
| OS: | UGOS Pro | 
| Internal File Systems: | BTRFS, EXT4 | 
| External File Systems: | EXT4, NTFS, FAT32, HFS+, ExFAT | 
| Maximum Capacity: | 8x 32TB HDD + 2x 8TB M.2 NVMe, plus external storage on USB or Thunderbolt | 
| Power: | 70.39W (drive access), 28.99W (drive hibernation) | 
| Dimensions: | 365 x 258 x 189 (mm) | 
Ugreen NASync DXP8800 Ultra: Design
- Unchanged chassis
- Room for 96GB
Since Ugreen first launched the DXP8800 Plus, I’ve been running that platform in my office, and almost nothing is wrong with the form factor or build quality. The DXP8800 Ultra inherits almost everything about the exterior and the drive bays.
The Ultra is built on the same thick aluminium chassis as the Plus, and it measures exactly the same dimensionally. The drive trays, rear dust filter, and dual 120mm fans all appear to carry over. Logically, if it isn’t broken, don't fix it.
On the Plus, I praised the numbered, lockable drive trays and the magnetic fan filter. We regretted that the trays were plastic, and that 2.5-inch drives need screws. But in reality, most people won’t be installing drives every day or using 2.5-inch media. Most people will use 3.5-inch HDDs, and for them the tool-less trays work perfectly well.
Comparing the two machines, the ports also sit where they did before. The front panel carries the power button, drive activity lights, an SD card reader, two Thunderbolt 4 ports and a USB 3.2 Gen 2 port.
Around the back are the PCIe slot, HDMI, a second USB 3.2 Gen 2 port, two USB 2.0 ports and the pair of 10GbE sockets. The card reader is now listed as SD 4.0. In retrospect, I’d have preferred that the Thunderbolt ports were on the back, since I use a Thunderbolt SSD, but that’s a personal choice.
Ugreen is more forthcoming about the PCIe slot this time. It lists it as Gen 4 x4, which matches what I’d always suspected on the Plus. That is plenty for a faster network card or a storage adapter. Fitting one still means removing the case feet and rear panel, so do it before you fill the bays with drives. Or, like me, find out the hard way.
Underneath, the small service panel hides two M.2 slots and two DDR5 SODIMM sockets. The Ultra ships with a single 8GB module, so one socket is free. A separate 128GB SSD holds the operating system, which isn’t accessible without more disassembly.
That leaves both M.2 slots for your own use. Ugreen lists 96GB as the maximum, which suggests a pair of 48GB modules. For reference, an unbranded 96GB kit (2x48GB modules) is about $1400 on Amazon.
There is still no laptop-style power brick, with the power supply being mounted internally. While this is preferable, because the PSU gets cooled inside the case, it does make a fully populated Ultra a heavy thing that you probably don’t want to move on your own. Before you add drives, it's not too difficult to pick up.
Overall, the Ultra inherits everything that made the Plus a masterclass in NAS hardware making. It is hard to fault, and just as hard to tell apart on the desk.
- Design: 4.5 / 5
Ugreen NASync DXP8800 Ultra: Features
- Intel Core 7 150U CPU
- Up to 96GB of memory
- Gen 4 PCIe slot
The Plus model ran on a Core i5 1235U, whereas the Ultra shifts to the Core 7 150U. Both are ten-core, twelve-thread mobile processors, with two performance cores and eight efficient ones. Core counts have not changed, so do not expect a massive leap in raw muscle.
What does change is the generation and the clock speed. The 150U is a 13th generation Raptor Lake part with a maximum turbo of 5.4GHz and a base frequency of 1.8GHz. The 1235U tops out at 4.4GHz and normally runs at only 1.3 GHz. The integrated graphics also grow, from 80 to 96 execution units. That should help with Quick Sync transcoding for Plex and Jellyfin, although the Plus coped well with Plex in my tests.
How much quicker is it? That depends entirely on the workload, since processing power doesn’t make SATA or the 10GbE LAN ports run any faster. As a computing platform, it’s probably 20% better overall, which might help Virtualisation and AI tasks, but the two chips are close cousins, so the 150U's advantage is more likely to show in lightly threaded jobs.
An annoyance for those who swear by ECC memory is that neither processor supports it. For a NAS aimed at teams and small businesses, that is a shame, and some buyers will not forgive it. The specifications suggest that ODECC (On-Die Error-Correcting Code) is supported, a built-in feature of DDR5 and LPDDR5 memory chips that automatically detects and corrects single-bit errors directly inside the individual RAM ICs. But this won’t be enough for those who like the extra check bits to stored data chunks on ECC RAM.
Today, non-ECC memory is expensive enough, and ECC RAM is even more expensive, so even if Ugreen had used a platform that supported ECC, many customers might have avoided it because of the high cost.
The Ultra ships with 8GB of DDR5 and supports up to 96GB, compared with a maximum of 64GB for the Plus. To clear up some confusion I've seen online, the RAM supplied in my DXP8800 Ultra was Samsung-branded 5600MHz, whereas the Plus model previously used 4800MHz RAM.
The faster memory offers a slight bandwidth advantage, but it's something to consider if you want to buy another module to pair with the pre-installed SODIMM. This chipset supports 4800MHz modules, so if you swap to a kit of, say, 16GB DDR5 SODIMMs at that speed, it should be fine.
Either way, 96GB is more memory than most NAS owners will ever need. Exceptions include those running ZFS under TrueNAS with a big cache, or those with a stack of virtual machines.
The PCIe slot is listed as Gen 4 x4. Four PCIe 4.0 lanes give a faster network card or storage adapter more than enough bandwidth. That’s enough bandwidth for four 10GbE LAN ports, or a low-profile video card for extra GPU power. The only caveats to installing a discrete video card in this system are that it must physically fit, work with PCIe 4.0, and have no extra PCIe power connectors, meaning it must run entirely off bus (slot) power.
Ugreen kept the rest of the connectivity unchanged, so the new chip supports the same devices as before.
- Features: 4.5 / 5
Ugreen NASync DXP8800 Ultra: Software
- UGOS Pro
- Docker and virtual machines
- Third-party OS sanctioned
The Ultra runs UGOS Pro, the same operating system used across the whole NASync range. In an earlier Ugreen review, I called it a work in progress. But it’s evolved since then into a clean, effective NAS environment that relies on Docker to run many critical applications, rather than software compiled specifically for this platform.
The pitch for the Ultra leans heavily on a direct teamwork ethos. It lists centralised management of files, users, permissions and devices, encrypted remote access, a firewall, encryption and backup across several platforms. There is a focus on Docker containers and virtual machines, which is where the Core 7 processing power and the extra memory prove their worth.
Some old complaints deserve a recheck. When I covered the Plus model, I noted that it missed two-factor authentication and WORM volumes that ransomware cannot alter. Also missing in action were the jumbo frames needed to fully exploit 10GbE ports. As UGOS Pro evolved, it has since added two-factor authentication, along with jumbo frames. However, WORM volumes are still missing, sadly.
The lack of Hybrid RAID was another grumble, and it appears to remain. Independent coverage says UGOS Pro still offers no flexible mixed drive mode, so unequal drives waste the difference. It also has no ZFS file system option, only Btrfs and EXT4.
If Ugreen added ZFS or something equivalent, it could hit the WORM drives and hybrid RAID issues over the head simultaneously.
One area where UGOS Pro leads the pack, rather than following, is the mobile app. It does nearly everything the web interface can, plus a few things it cannot. The Ultra shares the same software, so that strength carries over.
Another strength is that from relatively early on, Ugreen championed third-party operating systems, where other brands refused to accept them. It has said that installing one does not by itself change the hardware warranty, though it will not support problems the software causes, understandably.
But anyone heading down the third-party NAS path needs to be aware that while in the past two years some plugins have been crafted to control the fans and the front panel LEDs for the DXP6800 Plus and DXP8800 Plus, these have not been tested for the Ultra models at this time.
And for those who want to use Unraid, there is a licensing gotcha: the starter $49 option covers only six storage devices. That forces the use of the unlimited license for $109, even on the DXP6800 Plus, if you want to use all the bays and slots.
I’d love to have had the time to install a third-party NAS OS and test out if the Ultra machines will work with the Plus plugins created by the community, but alas, I like to produce more than one review each month.
UGOS Pro remains a work in progress, but it has rapidly become much closer to what TerraMaster and Asustor are fielding from a platform perspective. The Plus and the Ultra share it, so any future gains will benefit both.
- Software: 3.5 / 5
Ugreen NASync DXP8800 Ultra: Performance
- Faster CPU, same network
- M.2 slots are unchanged
- 10GbE x2 without extra hardware
On the Plus, testing shows that file serving over both 10GbE ports used less than 15 per cent of the processor, and on the Ultra that’s an even smaller proportion.
But for plain file serving, the Ultra would perform much like the Plus, because the 10GbE LAN port is the limiting factor, not the compute power behind it.
The extra processing power matters when the NAS does more than serve files. Containers, virtual machines, indexing, thumbnail generation and encrypted transfers all lean on the processor and memory. That is where the Ultra pulls ahead.
The network is the real limit. That is a best-case scenario, and a single client still tops out at the speed of one port, which is typically around 980MB/s. Early reviews of the Plus measured 650 to 700MB/s over 10GbE. On my Plus model, I often push 25GB files to it and get a sustained 980MB/s over a single 10GbE link. And, in my testing, the Ultra matched those numbers with four hard drives in a RAID 5 configuration and two SSDs used for caching that volume.
Those wanting faster transfer speeds have a few options, but these are the same ones the Plus hardware can also use. These include connecting to the NAS using the Thunderbolt port in host mode, which can establish a 40Gbps link.
Or you can use SMB to fuse the two 10GbE ports into one, with an appropriate switch. Or you could add a 40GbE LAN card to the PCIe slot, which would again need a switch capable of handling that much bandwidth.
All these things are possible with the Plus model, and remain unchanged in the Ultra.
On the Plus, M.2 slot one ran at full PCIe 4.0 speed, delivering well over 5500MB/s reads from a Gen4 x4 NVMe. Slot two managed less than half that amount, which indicated PCIe 3.0 with two lanes.
I didn’t expect this to change, because the new Core 7 150U processor doesn’t have any more PCIe lanes (20x) than the Core i5 1235U. And, predictably, inside the pocket where the RAM modules and NVMe drives live, the motherboard clearly marks one slot as Gen4 x4 and the other as Gen3 x2. So don’t mix them up, like I stupidly did.
Actually, it’s not a real issue, because UGOS Pro is smart enough to tell the module has moved and reconnect it to the system.
Eight hard drives at around 200MB/s each add up to roughly 1,600MB/s. That is close to what the slower M.2 slot throughput is, and well within reach of a pair of aggregated 10GbE ports. In practice, the drives and the network will limit the Ultra long before the processor does.
Noise deserves a mention, as Ugreen publishes no noise figure for the Ultra. Fully populated and in use, the volume was around 50 dBA, which is quiet enough for it not to be a massive annoyance.
Overall, using the supplied 8GB of RAM as a baseline, it would be hard to differentiate this from the Plus model. Those differences are only likely to surface if you have a particular workflow that involves Virtualisation, lots of Docker containers, or you are running an AI LLM locally. And, in all those situations, you will need more memory, and the 96GB this system can rock can truly come into play.
Ugreen NASync DXP8800 Ultra Final verdict
Where the DXP8800 Plus was a bolt from the blue, the DXP8800 Ultra’s arrival seems more measured. Ugreen kept everything that worked and refreshed the part that aged fastest, that being the processor, and with that change, it increased the memory ceiling.
So is it worth the extra money? For most buyers, sadly it probably isn’t. At today's prices, the Plus still gives you eight bays, two M.2 slots, dual 10GbE, dual Thunderbolt 4 and a PCIe slot for roughly $570 less. File serving, backups, media streaming and a handful of containers run happily on either. The Ultra's extra speed will rarely be the bottleneck unless you use it in specific ways.
That is someone running virtual machines, a large ZFS cache or a busy stack of containers, who will genuinely use more than 64GB of memory. It also suits those who expect to keep the NAS for five to ten years, where any advantage can be gained. For them, the extra headroom is cheap insurance against needing something more powerful in a couple of years.
Just budget for the memory, because DDR5 is not cheap this year. Should the RAM market return to where it was before the AI bubble, then the Ultra instantly becomes a much stronger option. And, as it’s hard to imagine that prices won’t eventually decline over time, making the Ultra a good call for the longer haul.
What’s mildly fascinating is that few alternative NAS units could even match the Plus model. The Synology DX1823xs+, for example, uses the AMD Ryzen V1780B, a four-core CPU, and supports up to 32GB of DDR4 ECC RAM, a single 10GbE LAN port, and eSATA expansion. Similarly, the TerraMaster T9-450 uses an Atom four-core processor, is also limited to 32GB, but at least has dual SFP+ 10GbE ports for close to $1200. But most 8-bay or larger options are pitched exclusively as file servers, while the DXP8800 series are something much more.
Two caveats apply. Neither the older Plus nor the new Ultra supports ECC memory, which will matter more to some businesses than any benchmark. And owners who want TrueNAS or Unraid will find the Plus better supported, at least initially.
If you are buying today, choose the Plus unless you have a clear or future use for 96GB. If street prices close the gap between this NAS and the Plus model to a couple of hundred dollars, the Ultra becomes an easy recommendation. Existing Plus owners should stay put. Nothing here justifies replacing a working NAS, and you could just be sticking your head in a bucket of bees.
If you want to save money on the NAS but don’t mind buying larger-capacity drives, the six-bay DXP6800 Ultra might be a good alternative, as it can also address 96GB of RAM.
Should you buy a Ugreen NASync DXP8800 Ultra?
| Value | Expensive when compared to the Plus | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Design | The design was strong and its almost entirely unchanged | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Features | 8-Bays, Dual 10GbE LAN and Dual Thunderbolt makes for a winning formula | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Software | Maturing of UGOS Pro, but it still needs WORM and hybrid RAID | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Performance | Slightly more power than before, and more RAM if you can afford it. | 4 / 5 | 
| Overall | One of the best NAS just got even better, but cost took its toll | 4 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You have a 5GbE or 10GbE network with dual 10GbE LAN ports, and with SMB Multichannel, you can distribute 20Gbps of data over a network easily. And with a PCIe slot, you can add more LAN bandwidth if you need it.
You need lots of RAM for VT or AI
Being able to scale to 96GB of memory enables this NAS to handle jobs that would break other devices. But, that much DDR5 might cost you almost as much as the NAS. 
Don't buy it if...
You are watching the budget
The Plus model isn't cheap, and the Ultra is more than $400 more. If you want to save money, the original Plus is a good choice, or consider six bays and the DXP6800 Ultra instead of the DXP8800 Ultra.
You already have a DXP8800 Plus
Unless you have a very specific problem that the DXP8800 Plus doesn't address, then moving from that to the Ultra would be a largely symbolic gesture. The Ultra adds slightly more processing power and enables an extra 32GB of RAM, and that's about it.

articles.title: Elon Musk vuelve a perder su estatus de billonario tres días después de conseguirlo
articles.text:
Elon Musk perdió su condición de billonario en dólares apenas tres jornadas después de haberla alcanzado, en medio de un desplome bursátil que afectó a sus dos principales empresas. El fundador de SpaceX y Tesla vio caer su patrimonio neto desde un máximo reciente de 1,05 billones de dólares el martes hasta 987.000 millones de dólares el jueves, según el índice de multimillonarios de Bloomberg.
La caída se produjo después de que las acciones de SpaceX retrocedieran un 3,5% y cotizaran por debajo de los 162 dólares, mientras que los títulos de Tesla bajaban más de un 2%. Según estimaciones de Forbes, Musk perdió 21.000 millones de dólares el miércoles por la mañana tras conocerse un informe según el cual la compañía aeroespacial planea reunir 40.000 millones de dólares para comprar chips de Nvidia.
Esa estrategia pudo haber generado inquietud entre los inversores por las necesidades de gasto y el nivel de endeudamiento de la empresa, en un momento en que destina fuertes sumas a infraestructura de inteligencia artificial.
Una semana de subidas y bajadas en Wall Street
El retroceso representa una pérdida de 63.000 millones de dólares apenas días después de que Musk recuperara el estatus de billonario el lunes, cuando las acciones de SpaceX subieron casi un 8% al inicio de la semana. Analistas de Morgan Stanley calificaron entonces la acción de “barata” a los precios de ese día.
Musk posee alrededor de 4.760 millones de acciones de SpaceX, a las que se suman otros 1.300 millones de acciones restringidas aún no consolidadas. Con ese respaldo accionario, su patrimonio neto había saltado de 976.900 millones a 1,04 billones de dólares tras la subida bursátil.
Pese a las oscilaciones, el empresario sigue siendo la persona más rica del mundo, con una diferencia de 600.000 millones de dólares respecto al segundo lugar.
Musk relativiza el peso de su fortuna
El propio Musk había advertido meses antes sobre la naturaleza de su riqueza, en una entrevista con el empresario Peter Diamandis realizada aproximadamente tres meses antes de que alcanzara por primera vez la condición de billonario, tras la salida a bolsa de SpaceX en junio.
“Billonario representa cierto porcentaje de propiedad en empresas que construí, y no es dinero que esté sentado en una cuenta bancaria”, afirmó Musk en esa conversación con Diamandis. El empresario agregó que el valor de su fortuna depende directamente del desempeño de sus compañías: “Poseo un porcentaje de las empresas. Las empresas hacen muchas cosas útiles, el valor de la empresa crece. Poseo un porcentaje de las empresas, y eso suma ese número, que parece alto”.
Según sus propias previsiones, dentro de diez años esa cifra podría no significar nada.
Otros multimillonarios enfrentan el mismo vaivén bursátil
Musk no es el único magnate tecnológico cuyo patrimonio fluctúa al ritmo del mercado de valores. El fundador de Oracle, Larry Ellison, le arrebató brevemente a Musk el título de hombre más rico del mundo el año pasado, después de que un reporte de ganancias excepcional disparara las acciones de la compañía un 36%. Ellison, de 82 años y dueño del 40% de Oracle, experimentó entonces un incremento patrimonial de 101.000 millones de dólares, pero perdió unos 34.000 millones apenas dos días después, mientras Musk ganaba 35.000 millones y recuperaba el primer puesto.
En sentido contrario, Michael Dell, propietario del 40% de su empresa homónima, sumó cerca de 122.000 millones de dólares entre septiembre de este año y el mismo mes de 2025, con lo cual casi duplicó su fortuna en un año. En ese mismo período, el patrimonio de Larry Page creció 16.300 millones de dólares, y el de Jeff Bezos aumentó 24.500 millones.

articles.title: Dormir 80 minutos menos durante seis semanas nos hace engordar, según un nuevo estudio
articles.text:
Dormir entre 7 y 8 horas es importante. Aunque no todos lo hagamos, es algo que tenemos bastante asumido. Aun así, no dejan de sorprendernos las nuevas consecuencias que se van descubriendo que podría acarrear descansar durante menos tiempo. Por ejemplo, según un estudio reciente, dormir poco podría hacernos engordar, con todo lo que eso conlleva.
Solo seis semanas. En este estudio participaron 95 personas con riesgo cardiometabólico elevado, que aseguraron dormir normalmente más de 7 horas. Durante seis semanas, algunos tuvieron que acostarse 90 minutos más tarde. Equivaldría más o menos a 80 minutos menos de sueño. Después, durante otras seis semanas, volvieron a su rutina de sueño habitual. Otros hicieron lo mismo, pero en orden inverso: primero el sueño adecuado y después el restringido. A lo largo de las 12 semanas que duró el estudio se analizaron tanto su sueño como su actividad mediante pulseras.
Además, se tomaron datos de su peso, la circunferencia de la cintura, la composición corporal y los niveles de hormonas asociadas al apetito. Al comparar todos estos datos, se vio que esas seis semanas fueron suficientes para alterar su peso.
Medio kilo. De media, los participantes ganaron una libra de peso, equivalente más o menos a medio kilo. Esto puede parecernos poco. Sin embargo, los autores del estudio recuerdan que solo se hizo un análisis de seis semanas. Si lo extrapolamos a un año entero, la ganancia de peso puede ser considerable. Lógicamente no será algo exacto, pero en las 52 semanas que tiene un año serían unos 4 kilos.
Un estudio más realista. En realidad, este no es el primer estudio que se ha llevado a cabo para estudiar cómo afecta dormir poco a la masa corporal. Sin embargo, en estudios previos se habían hecho restricciones muy drásticas del sueño. Normalmente, los participantes se despertaban tras 4 horas durmiendo. Esto es algo que, en nuestro día a día, no solemos mantener en el tiempo. Iríamos arrastrándonos por la vida. En cambio, dormir 5 o 6 horas es algo que muchas personas sí que mantienen de forma crónica. Por eso se decidió analizar cómo afecta al peso esa restricción más moderada del descanso.
También afecta al sedentarismo. Algo curioso que se vio en este estudio es que las personas obligadas a dormir menos fueron también más sedentarias durante su día. Incluso si se descontaban las horas extras que pasaban despiertos, su sedentarismo aumentó una media de 17 minutos al día. De nuevo puede parecer poco, pero se vio en un periodo corto de tiempo y al final todo suma.
Enfermedades asociadas. El aumento de peso y sedentarismo propician la obesidad y la aparición de enfermedades como la diabetes tipo 2 o las afecciones cardíacas. Por eso, dormir bien es importante por causas multifactoriales. Todo está relacionado.
Aún no se saben los motivos. A pesar de que las consecuencias son bastante llamativas, estos científicos no saben cuáles son las causas de esta relación. Aunque en el estudio se midieron algunos parámetros como las hormonas, no se conoce el mecanismo completo. Sí que es cierto que hay investigaciones anteriores en las que se ha visto que dormir poco puede aumentar la resistencia a la insulina, entre otros factores que también se relacionan con la obesidad y las patologías del corazón. Sin embargo, de nuevo, no sabemos qué relación hay entre el sueño y esa resistencia a la insulina.
Todo esto debe seguir estudiándose, especialmente en población general, no solo en personas que ya tienen cierto riesgo cardiometabólico. Mientras tanto, recuerda que dormir bien es importante por muchos motivos. Lo más evidente es que nos ayuda a estar más descansados durante el día, pero debemos prestar atención a todo lo demás.

articles.title: La France finance un consortium pour développer son cloud de confiance et son IA
articles.text:
L’État a accordé 20 millions d’euros du plan France 2030 au consortium formé par Cloud Temple, Thales, Bull, Vates et le CEA. D’ici fin 2028, les cinq partenaires doivent bâtir une offre française de cloud et d’intelligence artificielle pour héberger des données sensibles.
Marina Ferrari, alors secrétaire d’État au Numérique, a lancé le 22 mars 2024 à Strasbourg l’appel à projets « Renforcement de l’offre de services cloud », opéré par Bpifrance pour le compte de l’État. Seuls des fournisseurs de services cloud pouvaient prendre la tête des consortiums candidats, d’après le cahier des charges. Deux ans et demi plus tard, Cloud Temple a pris la tête du projet retenu et annoncé le 9 octobre. Les partenaires apporteront 27 millions d’euros en plus de l’aide publique, pour un budget total de 47 millions d’euros. « L’enjeu est désormais l’échelle », estime Sébastien Lescop, directeur général de Cloud Temple. Les cinq partenaires devront transformer leurs travaux en services vendus à des prix compétitifs, sur un marché tenu par les géants américains du cloud.
Une répartition des rôles sur fond d’obligation SecNumCloud
Les fournisseurs français multiplient depuis plusieurs mois les démarches pour obtenir SecNumCloud. OVHcloud a obtenu cette qualification pour son cloud public le 1er septembre, dix jours après l’entrée en vigueur de l’arrêté consacré à SecNumCloud 3.2. Avec ce texte signé le 12 août, le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu a rendu le référentiel de l’ANSSI obligatoire pour tout prestataire privé chargé des données les plus sensibles de l’État.
Cloud Temple détient cette qualification pour ses offres d’infrastructure et de plateforme. Avec ses quatre partenaires, l’hébergeur prévoit de développer des services de cloud et d’IA conformes aux exigences de NIS 2 ou de l’AI Act. Thales apporte au projet son expertise en cybersécurité et sa filiale de cloud de confiance S3NS. Google Cloud détient une part minoritaire de cette société, et SAP l’a retenue en avril pour faire tourner son ERP sous juridiction française.
Côté matériel, Bull assurera l’intégration des infrastructures destinées à l’IA avec sa plateforme logicielle maison, tandis que les chercheurs du CEA travailleront sur les architectures de nouvelle génération. Le socle de virtualisation open source sera fourni par Vates. Basé à Grenoble, cet éditeur développe la plateforme XCP-ng et a levé 30 millions d’euros auprès d’IRIS et de Bpifrance le 6 octobre, trois jours avant l’annonce du consortium.
Les fournisseurs français partagés sur le modèle du consortium
Devant la commission d’enquête de l’Assemblée nationale sur les dépendances numériques, le 21 avril, Sébastien Lescop a rappelé le recul des Européens sur le marché du cloud. Leurs fournisseurs en détenaient 27 % en 2017, contre 15 % au moment de l’audition. Philippe Latombe, président de la commission, a ensuite interrogé les fournisseurs sur les consortiums, après avoir constaté que les lauréats d’un appel d’offres de 180 millions d’euros de la Commission européenne avaient surtout candidaté en groupement.
« Chez Scaleway, nous n’y croyons pas. C’est trop compliqué », a répondu son directeur général, Damien Lucas. Ses clients cherchent d’après lui une alternative crédible à AWS ou à Azure, et non un assemblage de petites entreprises réparties entre l’infrastructure et les services managés. Philippe Miltin, directeur général d’Outscale, voulait pour sa part que l’État concentre ses aides sur quelques champions et cesse de les disperser.
Dans le groupement soutenu par France 2030, Cloud Temple pilote le programme et porte la majorité des travaux. Damien Lucas avait toutefois salué, lors de l’audition d’avril, l’appel à projets dont ce consortium est lauréat. Grâce à ce type d’aide, les fournisseurs peuvent selon lui continuer à développer de nouveaux produits. L’essentiel des investissements du secteur est consacré aux infrastructures, et le patron de Scaleway attend surtout des acheteurs publics des engagements de commandes pour les financer.

articles.title: Depuis que j’ai appris ce que signifie PPS sur un chargeur, je ne branche mon téléphone que s’il en est équipé
articles.text:
Depuis que j’ai appris ce que signifie PPS sur un chargeur, je ne branche mon téléphone que s’il en est équipé
Depuis que les fabricants ne glissent plus de chargeur dans la boîte, il faut l'acheter à part. Et là, tous les blocs ne se valent pas. Derrière l'USB-C universel se cache un détail décisif, la technologie PPS, qui ajuste la charge en temps réel pour préserver la batterie. Choisir le bon adaptateur n'est plus un luxe, c'est un geste de bon sens.
Vous déballez votre nouveau smartphone, vous soulevez le carton, et vous cherchez. En vain. Le petit bloc blanc qui accompagnait chaque téléphone a disparu, remplacé par un simple câble. Face au mur de chargeurs du magasin, tous estampillés USB-C à des prix allant du simple au décuple, une question se pose, que peu savent trancher : lequel choisir vraiment, et surtout, à quoi bon payer plus cher ?
Le port est universel, pas la charge
Depuis fin 2024, une directive européenne impose l'USB-C à tous les smartphones neufs, mettant fin à la jungle des connecteurs propriétaires. Conjuguée à la volonté des fabricants de réduire leurs coûts et leurs déchets, cette règle a un effet de bord : le bloc secteur a quitté la boîte. Le connecteur est donc le même pour tous. Mais c'est là que s'arrête l'uniformité. Car brancher une prise identique ne garantit pas la même charge.
Tout se joue dans le dialogue invisible entre le chargeur et le téléphone. Le standard qui régit cet échange s'appelle l'USB Power Delivery, ou USB-PD, aujourd'hui capable de monter jusqu'à 240 watts pour les ordinateurs portables. Mais le PD classique fonctionne par paliers fixes, par exemple 5, 9, 15 ou 20 volts. À chaque changement de palier, l'appareil doit encaisser un saut de tension, et le surplus d'énergie se dissipe en chaleur, l'ennemie numéro un de la batterie. C'est précisément ce défaut qu'une évolution du standard vient corriger.
PPS, le chargeur qui s'adapte en temps réel
Cette évolution porte un nom un peu abscons, PPS, pour Programmable Power Supply, soit alimentation programmable. Au lieu de sauter d'un palier à l'autre, un chargeur PPS ajuste sa tension et son courant en continu, par tout petits pas, pour coller au plus près des besoins réels de la batterie à chaque instant de la charge. Le téléphone et le chargeur négocient en permanence la dose d'énergie idéale, ni trop, ni trop peu.
Le bénéfice est double. D'abord la fraîcheur. En évitant les à-coups de tension, le PPS réduit nettement la chaleur produite pendant la charge. Or c'est la chaleur, bien plus que le nombre de cycles, qui use prématurément une batterie lithium. Un chargeur PPS ménage donc la longévité de l'accumulateur sur plusieurs années. Ensuite la vitesse : cette finesse de réglage autorise une charge à la fois plus rapide et plus douce. Le cas de Samsung est parlant. Pour atteindre sa charge "Super Fast Charging 2.0" à 45 watts sur un Galaxy haut de gamme, un simple chargeur 45 watts ne suffit pas, il lui faut impérativement la norme PPS capable de délivrer 5 ampères. Sans PPS, le téléphone se rabat sur une charge plus lente.
Bien choisir, et fuir les pièges
Reste à faire le bon achat, sans se tromper ni se faire avoir. Premier réflexe, ne pas surpayer des watts inutiles.
Anker Nano (45 W, écran intelligent)
Un chargeur plus puissant ne force jamais un téléphone à se charger plus vite : un mobile bridé à 25 watts ne tirera que 25 watts sur un bloc de 100 watts. Pour un smartphone, un modèle de 30 à 45 watts compatible PPS constitue le choix le plus pertinent, polyvalent et durable. Vérifiez donc la mention PPS sur l'emballage, et la puissance réellement acceptée par votre appareil.
Un second critère fait la différence, la technologie GaN, pour nitrure de gallium. Elle remplace le silicium dans les composants du chargeur et permet des blocs beaucoup plus compacts, plus efficaces et surtout moins chauds. Enfin, la prudence est de mise face aux modèles à bas prix d'origine douteuse. Un chargeur non certifié, dépourvu des protections contre les surtensions, les courts-circuits et la surchauffe, peut endommager la batterie, voire présenter un risque d'incendie. Cherchez le marquage CE, une marque reconnue et des certifications sérieuses. Payer un peu plus pour un bloc PPS et GaN certifié n'est pas une dépense superflue : c'est une assurance-vie pour un smartphone que l'on garde désormais plusieurs années.

articles.title: Planes de Microsoft 365 ahora tendrán solo la tercera parte de almacenamiento en la nube
articles.text:
Microsoft redujo el espacio de almacenamiento en OneDrive incluido en sus suscripciones Microsoft 365 Family y Premium, que pasó de un tope de 6 terabytes (TB) a solo 2 TB compartidos entre todos los usuarios de una misma cuenta.
El cambio, confirmado por la compañía en un documento de soporte técnico, implica que cada integrante de una familia tipo —hasta seis personas— recibirá en promedio unos 330 gigabytes (GB), frente al terabyte individual que recibía antes.
Cómo funcionaba el sistema anterior
Hasta ahora, cada plan Family o Premium otorgaba 1 TB de almacenamiento por usuario, con la posibilidad de compartir la suscripción con hasta cinco personas adicionales. Esa estructura permitía alcanzar un total de 6 TB cuando la cuenta estaba completa con sus seis miembros. Con el nuevo esquema, ese total se reduce a una bolsa compartida de 2 TB, independientemente de cuántos usuarios utilicen la cuenta.
Según explicó Microsoft en su documento oficial, “el suscriptor principal y hasta cinco miembros adicionales usan el mismo fondo de almacenamiento compartido en la nube”. La compañía aclaró además que, aunque la cuota de almacenamiento se comparte, los archivos de cada usuario permanecen privados entre sí.
El impacto varía según el número de usuarios
El ajuste no afecta a todos los suscriptores por igual. Quienes utilizan la suscripción en modalidad individual y antes estaban limitados a 1 TB ahora obtienen el doble de espacio, mientras que las cuentas compartidas entre dos personas no sufren una variación significativa. Sin embargo, las familias numerosas que repartían la suscripción entre tres o más integrantes enfrentan una reducción considerable en el espacio disponible por persona.
El plan Microsoft 365 Pro, por su parte, también sufrió una modificación: pasó de ofrecer 6 TB a un total de 5 TB compartidos. A diferencia de los otros dos planes, este conserva una proporción más cercana a la original.
Los precios no cambian pese al recorte
Pese a la reducción de espacio, Microsoft no ajustó el costo de ninguno de los tres planes. Microsoft 365 Family se mantiene en 12,99 dólares por mes o 129,99 dólares por año, mientras que Premium continúa en 19,99 dólares mensuales o 199,99 dólares anuales.
El plan Pro, que ahora ofrece 5 TB compartidos, sigue costando 99,99 dólares por mes, sin opción de pago anual, lo que lo convierte en una alternativa más de siete veces más cara que Family.
La compañía también precisó que es posible ampliar la capacidad mediante complementos de almacenamiento adicionales, aunque estos se destinan al fondo compartido y no a la cuota individual de cada usuario.
De acuerdo con el documento de soporte, “los complementos de almacenamiento adquiridos por los miembros de la suscripción se agregan automáticamente al fondo compartido”, al igual que los espacios gratuitos que algunos integrantes puedan tener por separado.
La nueva política de almacenamiento ya rige para los nuevos suscriptores de Microsoft 365 Family y Premium. En el caso de los clientes existentes, el cambio se aplicará recién en la primera renovación de su plan que ocurra en la fecha del 2 de mayo de 2027 o después. La compañía no precisó de qué manera se gestionarán los contratos de suscripción multianuales frente a esta transición.
Europa impulsa una alternativa a Microsoft 365 con enfoque en privacidad
En paralelo a los cambios en los planes de almacenamiento, la Unión Europea avanza con Office EU, una suite ofimática en la nube que busca posicionarse como alternativa a Microsoft 365.
Desarrollada por EUfforic Europe B.V., con sede en La Haya, la plataforma reúne herramientas como EU Docs, EU Spreadsheet, EU Presentation, EU Drive, EU Calendar, EU Email y EU Talk, compatibles con formatos como DOCX y XLSX. Su infraestructura es de código abierto y opera exclusivamente dentro de territorio europeo, sin transferir datos fuera de la Unión Europea, en cumplimiento con el Reglamento General de Protección de Datos (RGPD).
El proyecto, que se apoya en tecnologías como Nextcloud y Collabora Online, permite además importar documentos, correos y calendarios desde cuentas de Microsoft o Google para facilitar la migración. Por ahora, el acceso a Office EU es limitado y funciona mediante un programa de invitación anticipada que ya reúne a más de mil personas en lista de espera. La compañía todavía no reveló los planes de precios, que se darán a conocer a medida que avance el despliegue del servicio.

articles.title: Si la pregunta es si África tuvo un "rascacielos" hace 2.800 años, la respuesta de las matemáticas es que, técnicamente, sí
articles.text:
Cuando pensamos en rascacielos, es culturalmente inevitable asociarlos al Nueva York y Chicago de finales del siglo XIX y principios del XX con toda la razón del mundo, pero puede que existieran antes, muchísimo antes. Vamos, casi 3000 años antes y en un sitio a priori bastante insospechado, o esa es la conclusión a la que acaba de llegar un estudio realizado en Etiopía.
¿El primer rascacielos africano? Allá por el año 800 a. C., en Yeha, en la región de Tigray en el norte del mencionado país africano se levantó un palacio llamado Grat Be'al Gibri. Hoy está en ruinas, reducido a parte de la planta baja y poco más, como puedes ver en la imagen que ilustra este artículo. Tenía una planta de 60 metros de ancho por 60 metros de ancho y por aquel entonces, era el mayor edificio de este tipo conocido en el sur de Arabia y África oriental de la época
La pregunta del millón es: ¿qué altura tenía el templo? Un equipo multidisciplinar alemán se propuso resolver esa pregunta, así que se pusieron manos a la obra. La respuesta: en el peor de los casos, entre 16 y 19. Ojo, eso no quiere decir que las tuviera, solo que sus muros serían capaces de soportarlas.
Por qué importa. Hasta ahora, la altura de este tipo de edificios derruidos se deducía a partir de textos y pinturas, porque no había un análisis estructural que diera más pistas. Así, el historiador yemení al-Hamdānī (siglo X d. C.) habla de un palacio de 20 pisos en Yemen, y hay pinturas rupestres de Arabia del Sur que muestran palacios con al menos nueve.
El estudio propone además que quienes diseñaban y construían este tipo de edificios sabían lo que hacían, ya que los esfuerzos se reparten de forma moderadamente equilibrada entre los muros, lo que denota experiencia y conocimiento detrás.
UN VISTAZO A...
A prueba de milenios (y metros). El estudio de este yacimiento tiene más de un siglo de historia: comenzó con la Expedición Alemana a Aksum en 1906, siguió con excavaciones etíopo-francesas en 1971-73 y continúa desde 2009 con un proyecto etíopo-alemán financiado por la Fundación Alemana de Investigación (DFG). Los muros se hicieron con piedra, barro y vigas de madera, una técnica muy común hace unos 3.000 años en el sur de Arabia y el noreste de África, y que también se usaba en Grecia y Asia Menor desde la Edad del Bronce.
Como los rascacielos actuales (los de madera). Entre los trucos para su durabilidad y longevidad, para las vigas emplearon olivo africano y Cordia africana, resistente a las termitas (pero no al fuego). Entre las piezas más pesadas hay pilares monolíticos de arenisca de hasta 20 toneladas. Y pese a ser una construcción milenaria, la Universidad Técnica de Brandeburgo Cottbus-Senftenberg (BTU) compara su técnica con las construcciones híbridas de madera que hoy se proyectan en altura en ciudades como Sídney, Hamburgo o Berlín.
Cómo lo han calculado. Para llegar a esa conclusión, recrearon con un modelo tridimensional dos trozos de muro: una esquina y una puerta. Después, con software de modelado y análisis por elementos finitos, calcularon cuánto peso podía soportar, así que fueron añadiendo kilos al modelo hasta que el muro fallara.
Con valores medios, los muros habrían aguantado entre 48 y 56 plantas. En el peor de los casos, entre 16 y 19: 16 en el tramo de esquina y unas 19 en el de la puerta. Como curiosidad, la madera influyó muy poco: lo primero que cedía era el barro. Llegaron a una conclusión llamativa: los muros tenían capacidad de sobra, por lo que creen que solo algo excepcional pudo derrumbar el edificio. Lo más probable es que fuera el gran incendio que lo destruyó.
