articles.title: Scénario du pire : OpenAI et les labos s’entraînent en secret à la fin du monde — Frandroid
articles.text:
Les dirigeants de la Silicon Valley préparent déjà la fin du monde. En quelque sorte.
L’information vient d’Axios, dans une enquête de Maria Curi publiée le 9 octobre. Des cadres dirigeants d’Anthropic, d’OpenAI et d’autres entreprises du secteur font tourner des scénarios de « day after », le lendemain d’un premier incident grave attribué à une IA.
L’hypothèse jugée la plus probable est une cyberattaque de grande ampleur, capable de couper l’accès aux services bancaires, à Internet, voire à l’électricité et à l’eau.
Deux déclencheurs sont envisagés : un essaim d’agents autonomes qui s’échappe d’un environnement de test, ou un attaquant qui détourne des modèles déjà disponibles. Beaucoup d’experts interrogés par le média américain situent un tel événement dans les six à douze mois.
Un plan de crise tourné vers le Congrès
Simuler le pire n’a rien de surprenant, les armées et les banques le font depuis des décennies. Axios relève toutefois que beaucoup de chercheurs et de dirigeants du secteur tiennent l’incident pour inévitable.
Jusqu’à 330€ d’avantages avec nos offres Hello Prime ou Hello Prime Duo, dont 80€ cash à l’ouverture de compte !
    Pour aller plus loin
Pour Bill Gates, l’IA pourrait causer « un milliard de morts »
            
OpenAI confirme mener des exercices de préparation, tout en assurant que ces scénarios « ne sont pas traités comme inévitables ». Ce qu’Anthropic a refusé de commenter.
    Pour aller plus loin
C’est « la chose la plus dangereuse dont les humains se soient jamais approchés » : Bill Gates a radicalement changé d’avis sur l’IA
            
Et on a le contenu du pland. Cela comprend du red teaming, ces tests où l’on attaque son propre système, mais l’effort porte surtout sur la formation accélérée des élus du Congrès.
Les entreprises savent qu’aucune régulation ne passera à court terme et veulent peser sur les textes que Washington sortira après le choc.
    Pour aller plus loin
SpaceXAI va devenir SpaceXSI : Elon Musk adopte la « super intelligence » chère à Donald Trump
            
Leurs stratèges tablent sur des démocrates renforcés par les élections de mi-mandat du 3 novembre et pressés de sévir. Certaines propositions du parti vont jusqu’à interdire la superintelligence ou suspendre le développement des modèles avancés, quand un « kill switch » obligatoire trouve des soutiens dans les deux camps.
    Pour aller plus loin
« Aucune pression concurrentielle américaine ne devrait justifier l’imprudence » : Sam Altman veut ralentir l’IA, la Maison Blanche préfère la course avec la Chine
            
Les deux laboratoires cités ont eux-mêmes documenté le risque qu’ils redoutent. Le 1er septembre, OpenAI a classé Astra comme son premier modèle au seuil « critique » en cybersécurité : avec les bons outils, il trouve des failles inconnues et les exploite sur des systèmes bien protégés sans qu’un humain guide chaque étape.
    Pour aller plus loin
GPT-6 Astra : OpenAI lance son modèle le plus puissant et annonce « l’ère de l’AGI »
            
Anthropic a lancé sa Cyber Mission le 8 octobre, la veille du scoop, avec onze partenaires dont CrowdStrike, Dragos et Palo Alto Networks pour sécuriser réseaux électriques et distribution d’eau. L’entreprise prévoit que l’IA avantagera les défenseurs d’ici deux ans et admet que ce n’est pas forcément le cas d’ici là.
Ce que le scoop ne dit pas
On ne connaît ni le détail de ces plans, ni l’identité des sources, ni la façon dont l’échéance a été estimée. Et cela concerne avant tout les Américains.
Pour nous, il reste à savoir ce que vaudrait une loi votée à Washington face à une attaque montée ailleurs.
Les modèles à poids ouverts, téléchargeables librement, échappent déjà à tout bouton d’arrêt. En Europe, l’AI Act oblige depuis août 2025 les fournisseurs de modèles à risque systémique à signaler les incidents graves, ce qui règle la paperasse et pas grand-chose d’autre.
    Pour aller plus loin
L’AI Act est adopté : l’intelligence artificielle va changer dans l’Union européenne
            
Il faut aussi regarder à qui profite la fuite. Un secteur qui annonce lui-même sa catastrophe, calendrier à l’appui, se pose en interlocuteur obligé des élus le jour venu. Sam Altman, patron d’OpenAI, aurait d’ailleurs déclaré début octobre à Politico que le monde devrait accepter que de mauvaises choses arrivent en échange des bénéfices de l’IA.
Prévoir le lendemain d’un accident, personne ne peut reprocher ça à des industriels ni à des États. Ce qui me gêne tient au rôle que ces entreprises se réservent : elles développent les modèles qui rendent l’attaque possible et veulent influencer fortement les ois.

articles.title: Gaming consoles are more expensive than ever, and fewer people are buying them
articles.text:
Bottom line: The US console market is slowing, and more expensive hardware is making it harder to attract buyers. Consumers bought 559,000 consoles in August, down 15% from a year earlier and the lowest August total since 2013, according to figures shared by Circana's Mat Piscatella. The average selling price rose from $476 in 2025 to $541 in 2026.
For manufacturers, those higher prices can soften the financial impact of falling sales. Sony's PlayStation hardware revenue increased 17% year over year, even though unit sales declined 11%. Higher-tier models helped make up the difference.
But the figures also show the limits of mid-generation upgrades. More expensive machines allow manufacturers to generate additional revenue without necessarily expanding the audience for their hardware.
Console prices are at historical highs, driven by pressure on component costs and the introduction of premium models such as the $900 PS5 Pro. That leaves buyers facing a higher cost of entry than in previous console cycles.
The slowdown extends across all three major manufacturers. Xbox unit sales fell 31% year over year, reaching their lowest August level since 2020. Nintendo unit sales declined 15% from August 2025.
The average price a consumer has paid for a new Xbox console in 2026 YTD ending August is $529, 26% higher than a year ago, while the average PlayStation console has sold for $597, 20% higher than last year. Both prices are at all-time US highs. Price sensitivity is becoming a real problem.
– Mat Piscatella (@matpiscatella.bsky.social) October 9, 2026 at 9:02 AM
The PS5 and Xbox Series X|S are roughly six years into their generation, and market saturation is likely contributing to weaker demand. Price increases earlier in 2026 also affected when consumers bought their machines. A rush to buy consoles before the hikes took effect brought sales forward, reducing the pool of potential summer buyers.
The result is a hardware market in which upgrades and higher prices have failed to prevent falling unit sales. Sony's revenue growth shows that selling more expensive models can help a manufacturer, but it does not indicate broader growth in console ownership.
The comparison with 2013 highlights another difference. That August, US console sales totaled 423,000 units as the PS3 and Xbox 360 approached the end of their generation. Buyers were preparing for the PS4 and Xbox One, both due that November.
This time, no successor machines have been officially unveiled. The current slowdown is occurring without an announced generation of replacement hardware on the horizon.
Software sales show a similar gap between an overall figure and the changes beneath it.
Year-to-date spending on new physical games rose 5% to $738 million. Yet spending on traditional physical formats, including discs and full-data cartridges but excluding Switch 2 Game-Key Cards, fell 3%.
Game-Key Cards accounted for the difference. Spending on those releases increased 631%, enough to bring the physical software category into positive territory.
That percentage reflects the format's relatively small presence in 2025 and its wider adoption by major publishers in 2026. It does not represent a comparable rebound in traditional physical media, which continue to lose ground as players move to digital storefronts.
The Switch 2 also helped change the August sales rankings. Elden Ring rose from 41st in July to seventh following its Switch 2 port. NBA 2K27 was the month's best-selling game and ranked third for 2026 so far. Madden NFL 27 finished second in August.
Across the broader games market, August content spending fell 10% year over year to $3.8 billion. Year-to-date spending reached $32.2 billion, down 2%.
Mobile spending dropped 18%, the largest decline among the reported platforms. Console content spending fell 7%, while PC gaming spending increased 13%. Subscription purchases also grew, rising 3%.
The PC platform's growth stood out in a month when both console hardware purchases and overall content spending declined. Meanwhile, higher-priced consoles and Game-Key Cards supported revenue in specific categories without reversing the wider slowdown.

articles.title: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?
articles.text:
At this year’s OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman unveiled the company’s new AI agent Dots — and told the crowd that the company wants to “set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI.” OpenAI would spend the day taking veiled shots at Meta’s Muse, its primary competitor, for failing to keep users’ data safe. Yet Muse itself, a couple of months earlier, had launched as a supposedly safer alternative to predecessor OpenClaw — with CEO Mark Zuckerberg promising it was “built from the ground up for privacy and security.”
AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?
Meta positioned its Muse agent as a safer alternative to OpenClaw. OpenAI promises Dots is a safer alternative to Muse.
In an age when companies hoard customers’ personal data and cyberattacks are a dime a dozen, AI labs are trying to convince users to share even more information with their agents. Their latest strategy for success is one-upping the competition by promising that unlike their rivals, they’ll keep user data away from prying eyes. The question is whether companies can keep these promises.
Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, wrote on X that the company’s “goal with muse was to build something like openclaw that we could make safe and secure and easy to use and scale to billions of people.” User data is stored on a secure VM, what Zuckerberg described as an “isolated linux computer with a browser, CPU, memory, and storage.” The company said that most of the effort in building Muse was related to “careful design and engineering to operate [it] more safely.” Meta’s blog post continued, “Muse can and will still make mistakes, but we expect they’ll be much less frequent and cause much less damage due to the safety systems we’ve built in.”
But though Muse topped the App Store charts and, per Apptopia, gained 600,000 daily active users in the US within weeks, Meta’s promises seem to have fallen short. Although data is isolated from other users, and the company plans to introduce a way “to cryptographically and verifiably prevent Meta from accessing data in your VM” later this year, Meta itself can still access the data. A security researcher quickly exposed a zero-day vulnerability that could allow someone to take control of Muse (which has since been patched), raising fears of outside attacks. Multiple serious security issues reportedly cropped up at the last minute before launch, one of which could have allowed users to access Meta’s own internal databases, per 404 Media.
Muse also appears to liberally collect (and in some cases, hand out) data. It defaults to allowing Meta to train models on what users put into it, though it’s possible to opt out. An Inc. reporter complained that Muse uploaded and read his private messages without him asking it to, and a YouTuber said it had offered his address to a stranger via Marketplace — in both cases, Muse was functioning apparently as intended, but the user didn’t realize how far it would go. The platform creates “detailed profiles of all your friends and family,” as Wired reported. None of this is necessarily unexpected from Meta, but it certainly doesn’t back up the idea that Muse is uniquely privacy- or security-conscious.
OpenAI seized on this fact when announcing Dots in late September. Alexander Embiricos, OpenAI’s Codex product lead, said onstage at DevDay that OpenAI is focused on having the “most trustworthy, safe, and secure assistant,” and CEO Sam Altman demonstrated ways that people could exert control over their individual Dots, such as setting a rule that it should never make a purchase over a certain dollar amount. “I think we’re in a different position to Meta in that they don’t have an AI product that has 1.2 billion users,” said Glen Coates, OpenAI’s head of app platform, adding that “launching something that makes those kinds of mistakes is something that we would try to take the care to avoid.”
Altman himself also pushed the privacy angle at DevDay. To court business customers, executives presented a framework allowing enterprises to have “stronger controls” over their data and zero data retention policy options (meaning no data is stored on OpenAI servers). Indeed, so far, there haven’t been many privacy scandals with Dots — although since it’s only available on the $100-and-up ChatGPT subscription tiers, there are also likely fewer people using it.
People may still not feel comfortable giving OpenAI their personal data, in part simply because AI agents require so much of it. For instance, The Verge’s Allison Johnson felt uncomfortable typing in her bank information when the bot asked as part of a relevant task (Muse has a Stripe integration to take care of that).
Not all companies are making privacy promises, of course. Instinct was publicly criticized for reportedly overly-broad terms of service that gave it unfettered access to data; since then, the company seems to have made adjustments. For now, AI labs seem to be counting on a three-part approach to popularizing AI agent use with the general public: Make them useful, make them cute and disarming to help offset the creepiness, and make promises about privacy — and hope they hold up.

articles.title: 730 millions de données volées : la police fait tomber Reacher, le moteur de recherche pirate de 3 ados
articles.text:
Un nouveau site pirate vient de tomber en France. Ce mardi 6 octobre, l’Office anti-cybercriminalité (OFAC) a interpellé trois administrateurs présumés de Reacher, qui a été rebaptisé Stryx au début de l’été. Pour rappel, un lookup est un moteur de recherche qui recense et revend des données personnelles issues de fuites et de piratages.
Trois mineurs de 17 ans à l’origine du site
Les trois suspects sont des mineurs de 17 ans, jusqu’ici inconnus de la justice. Ils sont soupçonnés de recel d’extraction frauduleuse de données, de détention et de transmission frauduleuse de données, en bande organisée. Ils encourent jusqu’à dix ans de prison. Leur procès est prévu en janvier 2027. Notez que ce n’est pas la première fois que de très jeunes pirates se retrouvent dans le viseur des autorités françaises. En juin, la France avait déjà arrêté sept jeunes hackers après plus de 1 500 cyberattaques perpétrées sur le territoire.
Créé en mars 2026, Stryx revendiquait 730 millions de lignes de données indexées, et affichait plus de 3 millions de requêtes. On tapait une information quelconque et le site renvoyait tout ce qu’il savait sur la personne. Il suffisait d’un nom, d’un numéro de téléphone, d’un IBAN ou même d’une plaque d’immatriculation. L’accès était gratuit ou sur abonnement, et les utilisateurs pouvaient acheter des crédits supplémentaires pour faire plus de recherches.
L’enquête a été ouverte le 15 mai, après un signalement de l’association e-Enfance. Dans la foulée de l’opération, les données des administrateurs, des clients et des utilisateurs du service ont été collectées, et les policiers sont en train de les analyser. Les utilisateurs de Reacher pourraient donc eux aussi se retrouver dans le viseur de la justice.
À lire aussi : De « nombreuses plaintes » – la CNIL dénonce l’explosion des « Google » des fuites de données
Les « lookups » dans le viseur de la police française
Reacher n’est pas un cas isolé. Les plateformes de ce type, souvent décrites comme des « Google » des fuites de données, sont dans le collimateur des autorités depuis plusieurs mois. En mai, un jeune de 19 ans a été mis en examen et placé en détention provisoire pour avoir créé et administré le site « C3N Backup ». Plus récemment, BrixHub, qui revendique 11 milliards de données, a fait réagir la ministre chargée du Numérique, Anne Le Hénanff. Le 5 octobre, celle-ci a signalé le lookup à la justice, dans l’intention de faire fermer le site.

articles.title: Spy X Family tome 17 : où précommander l’édition collector ?
articles.text:
Après le coffret collector du tome 15 et l’édition spéciale du tome 16, Kurokawa propose un nouveau coffret pour le tome 17 de Spy x Family. Proposé au prix de 24,95 €, ce coffret collector accompagne l’édition classique du manga, vendue à 7,30 €. Les précommandes sont notamment ouvertes chez Amazon et Fnac, en attendant la sortie prévue le 12 novembre 2026.
Spy x Family
Auteur : Tatsuya Endo
Éditeur : Kurokawa
Date de parution : 12 novembre 2026
Nombre de pages : 224 pages
Format : Manga broché
Prix : 24,95 € (édition normale : 7,30 €)
Cette édition spéciale comprend le tome 17 du manga, accompagné d’une jaquette alternative, ainsi que plusieurs accessoires réunis dans un coffret. Les fans retrouveront un bonnet et une paire de lunettes de soleil, deux objets qui rappellent les déguisements et les identités de couverture employés par la famille Forger pour préserver leurs secrets. Cette édition collector contient également un puzzle de 90 pièces, une carte à gratter et une planche de stickers.
Affiché à 24,95 €, ce coffret s’adresse à celles et ceux qui souhaitent compléter leur collection avec des objets dérivés du manga. Il coûte 17,65 € de plus que l’édition classique également en précommande, soit plus de trois fois son prix.
On en est où, dans l’histoire de Spy x Family ?
Attention, quelques éléments de contexte sur l’intrigue des précédents tomes.
Dans Spy x Family, Loid Forger, alias Twilight, est un espion chargé d’une mission délicate : approcher Donovan Desmond, une figure politique importante, afin de préserver la paix entre les nations rivales. Pour réussir, il doit se construire une famille de toutes pièces. Il adopte Anya, une petite fille capable de lire dans les pensées, puis épouse Yor, qui mène elle aussi une double vie de tueuse à gages.
Si les trois personnages jouent la comédie au quotidien, leurs secrets respectifs alimentent les situations les plus improbables de la série. Anya, qui connaît les véritables identités de ses parents adoptifs, doit notamment éviter de révéler ce qu’elle sait.
Dans le tome 17, les relations au sein du couple Forger prennent une place importante. Après avoir longtemps gardé ses interrogations pour elle, Yor décide de parler à Loid. Les deux personnages choisissent alors de sortir ensemble, une occasion pour Yor de mieux comprendre ses propres sentiments. En parallèle, le cahier de Melinda Desmond révèle des liens entre Donovan et des personnes inattendues, susceptibles d’apporter de nouveaux éléments à la mission de Twilight.
Ce dix-septième volume fait avancer à la fois la relation entre Loid et Yor et l’intrigue d’espionnage qui se cache derrière leur vie de famille en apparence ordinaire.

articles.title: Moins de 100 euros pour un smartphone, c'est possible grâce à cette réduction sur l'Oppo A5 — Frandroid
articles.text:
L’Oppo A5 est un smartphone d’entrée de gamme conçu pour tenir la route. Pour tenir son prix, la marque chinoise a dû faire des choix. Ce smartphone mise donc sur une batterie endurante et une bonne résistance aux chutes, mais pèche sur la qualité de son écran. Néanmoins, avec la promotion offerte par son constructeur qui le passe sous les 100 euros, il devient encore plus intéressant.
Nous recommandons l’Oppo A5 pour…
- Sa batterie endurante de 6 000 mAh
- Sa charge rapide de 45 watts
- Sa résistance aux éclaboussures et aux chutes
Déjà attractif avec son prix habituel de 149,90 euros, l’Oppo A5 est encore plus intéressant en ce moment puisqu’il passe à 99,90 euros sur le site de la marque.
Un smartphone endurant et résistant
Côté design, l’Oppo A5 mise sur un dos mat à l’effet brumeux, d’où le nom de son coloris Blanc brumeux. Un coloris Violet de minuit existe aussi, mais il est actuellement en rupture de stock.
Parmi les très bons points de cet Oppo A5, il y a l’autonomie. Avec une capacité de 6 000 mAh, le constructeur chinois annonce un peu plus de 16 heures de streaming vidéo sur YouTube, un chiffre mesuré en laboratoire. De quoi tenir une journée, voire plus selon votre utilisation. Côté recharge, la charge rapide de 45 watts permet de passer de 0 à 100 % en 84 minutes selon Oppo (et à 30 % en 21 minutes).
Avec une telle autonomie, il a sa place dans le sac de randonnée. Il est aussi certifié IP65, ce qui le protège de la poussière et des projections d’eau (pluie, éclaboussures), mais pas d’une immersion. Oppo indique par ailleurs qu’il a passé en laboratoire les tests de chute et de chocs de la norme militaire MIL-STD-810H, sans préciser de hauteur de chute. L’écran est protégé par un verre doublement trempé qui, selon Oppo, résiste 160 % mieux aux chutes que celui de l’Oppo A3, la génération précédente.
Des performances honnêtes pour ce prix
Les bordures de cet écran sont assez épaisses, ce qui n’est plus vraiment dans l’air du temps. L’Oppo A5 dispose d’un écran LCD de 6,67 pouces, en 720p et à 90 Hz, avec un pic de luminosité annoncé à 1 000 nits. Sur le papier, c’est suffisant pour garder l’écran lisible en extérieur, sans faire de miracle en plein soleil. Par ailleurs, Oppo a fait en sorte que l’écran tactile reste utilisable même si vous portez des gants.
À l’intérieur, Oppo a opté pour le Snapdragon 6s 4G Gen 1, une puce limitée à la 4G (pas de 5G ici), et pour 4 Go de RAM. Celle-ci est extensible, mais attention, vous allez puiser dans un espace de stockage de 128 Go (qu’une carte microSD permet heureusement d’agrandir). Cette configuration suffit pour vos besoins quotidiens, que ce soit pour scroller sur les réseaux sociaux ou pour regarder une série en streaming. Sans surprise, il va montrer ses limites sur les jeux les plus gourmands en ressources.
Ce smartphone fonctionne avec ColorOS 15 qui possède plusieurs fonctionnalités IA pratiques, notamment en photo, puisque vous pourrez renforcer la netteté de vos clichés ou effacer certains éléments.
Les bons smartphones à 100 euros se font de plus en plus rares. Si vous voulez voir d’autres modèles au même prix que cet Oppo A5, rendez-vous dans notre guide des smartphones à moins de 100 euros.

articles.title: SPECviewperf 15.0.1 Linux Edition Released: Linux's Key Graphics Benchmark Adds Arm Support
articles.text:
A couple of weeks back, the Standard Performance Evaluation Corporation released a new Linux version of SPECviewperf, the consortium’s workstation graphics benchmark. Now up to version 15.0.1 and the group’s first Linux Edition release in almost half a decade, the new release gives the Linux graphics benchmark a significant facelift in both the features it offers and the workloads it tests.
Despite the long gap between Linux Edition releases, the timing of this new release could not be better. Beyond a slew of updates to the venerable Linux graphics benchmarking suite, including workload updates and a whole new GUI, the latest version of SPECviewperf adds Arm AArch64 support, marking the first time the graphics benchmark has been natively available on any Arm-based system. Consequently, the Linux version of the benchmark is treading new ground for SPECviewperf, something it rarely gets to do, giving us valuable first-look insights into how well Arm devices can handle traditional workstation graphics workloads.
We, of course, could not help ourselves and decided to take some time looking at the newest Linux benchmark and how it runs on some of our most recent Arm-based boxes. So, without further ado, let us jump right in.
SPECviewperf 15.0.1 Linux Edition Highlights
SPEC has offered a Linux version of its workstation graphics benchmark suite for nearly a decade, first releasing a Linux build in 2019 with SPECviewperf 13. Because many CAD, CAM, and 3D rendering workstation applications are OpenGL-based (or not available on Linux at all), the consortium has ported its graphics workloads to Linux to provide a counterpart to the Windows version. The net result is that the Linux version supports a smaller set of workloads overall (there is no DirectX here, for a start), but it still offers a solid look at workstation performance on Linux.
All told, the Linux Edition of SPECviewperf 15.0.1 offers 8 of the Windows suite’s 11 benchmarks, including graphics traces from Blender 3.6, 3DEXPERIENCE CATIA/CATIA V5, Creo 9, Maya 2025, Solidworks 2024, NX 2406, and visualizations from OpendTect and the Tuvok library. Compared with the previous version of the suite, 2020 3.0, the Blender workload is new, while CATIA, Creo, Maya, Solidworks, and NX workloads have all been updated, as they were in the Windows version released last year.
Notably, this year’s release of the benchmark suite also gets a newer GUI with more features, bringing more graphical controls and an improved setup routine to the workstation graphics benchmark.
That new GUI goes hand-in-hand with the ability to download and install just a fraction of the benchmark suite’s workloads, which, when fully installed, take up nearly 100GB of space. SPEC calls this their “snap-in” architecture, which makes each workload a snap-in element of the suite rather than one monolithic suite. It also lets system vendors and other operators more easily test only the graphics workload(s) they care about.
But arguably the marquee feature is support for AArch64 systems, marking the first time SPECviewperf has been natively available for an Arm-based architecture. The fundamental concept of replying OpenGL traces remains unchanged, as SPECviewperf is a graphics benchmark rather than a full-scope application benchmark, but that playback system can now operate under AArch64 and help to expose how well the graphics hardware and associated graphics drivers perform under Linux.
Speaking of hardware and drivers, the Linux benchmark suite supports a narrower range than Windows. While the Linux version of SPECviewperf 15.0.1 can run on any system with an OpenGL 4.5-compliant GPU, in practice it supports only AMD and NVIDIA GPUs, leaving Intel as the odd one out. On the plus side, it supports integrated GPUs, which is extremely helpful for testing the companies’ recent high-performance SoCs, including AMD’s Strix Halo and NVIDIA’s GB10.
SPECviewperf 15.0.1 Linux Edition Performance
With SPEC’s latest Linux graphics benchmark in hand, we wasted no time loading it on some of our recent Linux systems to look at performance. Getting true apples-to-apples performance here is a bit difficult since few chips/systems fall into identical weight classes, but it is still an interesting look.
Specifically, we ran the benchmark on a couple of our Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo boxes), the Dell Pro Max with GB10 (based on the NVIDIA GB10), and, for a high-end workstation, a Threadripper 9980X system with a Radeon AI Pro R9700 installed.
We will start things with a focus on mini-PCs. Under Linux, we find that performance is heavily in AMD’s favor here. Both Strix Halo boxes are performing far better than the GB10-based box, often by a factor of 2x or more.
Our GB10 machines are set up for AI workloads in a cluster, and are Arm-based. At the same time, we would be remiss not to consider how well (or poorly) NVIDIA’s Linux drivers are optimized here, since GB10’s graphics performance under Linux has not been a major focus until now. Take this more as a run just to validate that the Linux suite worked on the platforms, rather than being an ideal benchmark between all of them.
Still, for the moment it is a feather in AMD’s cap. Especially for ASRock Industrial’s AI BOX-A395, which remains the fastest Strix Halo box to cross our lab desks.
Meanwhile, to put those AMD iGPU results in context of what a more powerful discrete desktop system can do, here is a look at their performance plotted next to the results for our Threadripper + Ryzen AI Pro system. It is actually closer than you might first expect: most of the time the Strix Halo systems deliver around half of the performance of the high-end R9700 discrete video card. More surprisingly, they outperformed the discrete card in the NX 2406 workload.
So far, the focus on Strix Halo boxes such as AMD’s own Ryzen AI Halo system has been on AI development for obvious reasons, but these benchmarks also show the boxes can be reasonably performant for workstation graphics tasks, as long as the CPU doesn’t become the bottleneck first.
Final Words
Overall, the release of the Linux Edition of SPECviewperf 15.0.1 comes at an opportune time for the industry, as well as ServeTheHome. As the industry’s de facto benchmark for workstation graphics workloads, SPECviewperf carries an immense amount of weight within the industry. And by refreshing the benchmark suite to not only bring its workloads up to date with its Windows counterparts, but also adding Arm AArch64 support for the first time, this gives everyone a very valuable initial look into the workstation graphics performance of the recent slate of Arm-based mini-PCs that have been hitting the professional market.
As for ServeTheHome, we have been reviewing new hardware, including GB10-based boxes and AMD’s Radeon AI Pro R9700 video card, so the release of a Linux benchmark suite is well timed for us. Especially as we are fond of testing under Linux for a multitude of reasons. So do not be surprised if you see SPECviewperf pop up in some future reviews as one of our GPU benchmarks.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s Grok Bot will pick Claude over Grok when it’s better. One-model loyalty is dead.
articles.text:
Elon Musk’s Grok Bot will pick Claude over Grok when it’s better. One-model loyalty is dead.
I’m Matt Burns, Chief Content Officer at Insight Media Group. Each week, I round up the most important AI developments, explaining what they mean for people and organizations putting this technology to work. The thesis is simple: workers who learn to use AI will define the next era of their industries, and this newsletter is here to help you be one of them.
Elon Musk posted an “important note” on Wednesday about Grok Bot, the AI agent SpaceX launched in beta in August: “Important note regarding Grok @Bot: Going forward, @SpaceX will use the best back end model for any given task, including Claude Opus 5.5, MidJourney, Suno and other leading APIs. Whatever is most likely to give you the best outcome.”
Grok Bot is a joint product of SpaceXAI, the Musk AI lab now folded into SpaceX, and Cursor, which SpaceX agreed in June to buy for $60 billion in stock, a deal that closed in August.
In August, I wrote that when models converge on price, the money moves to whoever decides which model gets the job. This trend is happening across organizations increasingly relying on AI and trying to balance rising costs.
I heard this firsthand this week. At least 10 of the 22 company leaders we interviewed at an AI event this week described the same habit: pick the model by the task, and keep the expensive one for the work that needs it.
Model triage is how companies are controlling AI costs
I’m in New York City this week with Alex Wilhelm of the Cautious Optimism newsletter and Nick Lucchesi of The New Stack, and we spent Monday and Tuesday at Insight Partners’s ScaleUp:AI conference interviewing the people running 22 of Insight’s portfolio companies. Please note, Insight Partners owns The New Stack, and we shot these interviews for a video series Insight is producing. I’m not naming anyone here or pushing any of their products. These are real companies run by experienced operators, and what they told us about running AI matches what the rest of the market is doing, as the OpenRouter numbers below show.
The most common model triage setup we heard about was a funnel. One security company runs a rules engine over everything first and passes what survives to small models. Larger models only see what’s left. One of its executives told us that running a petabyte of data through any model, even a small one, would cost millions of dollars. Another company runs requests to its agent through a cheap model to figure out what the user wants before the expensive model does anything.
Cost was the reason most of them gave. One executive said his company started with unlimited AI budgets and is now asking what all those tokens actually bought. Another said his employees kept reaching for the most advanced model even when it was overkill, so the company now teaches staff which model fits which job. A third put the incentive bluntly: The labs do better when you spend more tokens. Of course, a couple of the people we talked to sell small models for a living, so I’m weighing their enthusiasm accordingly.
Switching has its own risk. One engineering leader told us his team swapped in a newer model three days before a demo for an important prospect because the benchmarks said it was cheaper and just as good. The workflow broke, and his team rolled back over a weekend. His lesson was evals, a set of tests that would have caught the problem before his team had to find it by hand. The New Stack’s Amanda Caswell found the vendor version of that story last month, when Anthropic made Opus 5.5 20% cheaper than Opus 5 and broke four things agents depend on.
In short, test before you switch, and follow the ABS rule: Always Be Switching.
OpenRouter’s leaderboard shows cheap models doing the volume
OpenRouter is a service developers use to reach hundreds of models through one connection, and it publishes what flows through it. In the week through October 7, four of its ten most-used models were “Flash” models, the cheap, fast versions labs ship alongside their flagships. Anthropic just made its own cheap tier cheaper. Haiku 5.5 launched Wednesday at $.10 per million input tokens, a 90% cut for requests under 100,000 tokens, and small models like it typically handle high-volume jobs like classification and routing.
Cheap models carry the volume. The frontier model is growing fastest.
Selected models from OpenRouter’s top 10 by tokens processed in the week through Oct. 7, 2026, and the change from the week before.
| Model | Maker | Tokens | Change | 
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash | DeepSeek | 33.6T | +48% | 
| GLM 5.3 Flash | Z.ai | 10.5T | -1% | 
| MiMo-V2.6-Flash | Xiaomi | 10.1T | +11% | 
| GPT-6 Luna | OpenAI | 6.46T | +28% | 
| Claude Opus 5.5 | Anthropic | 3.37T | +74% | 
| Jev 1.13 | TypeSafe | 3.32T | +12% | 
Source: OpenRouter rankings, licensed CC BY 4.0. Tokens count prompt and completion tokens routed through OpenRouter and don’t measure users or spend. Rows shown are Nos. 1, 3, 4, 6, 9 and 10; No. 2 is an unattributed stealth model.
The frontier model is growing too. Claude Opus 5.5 is ninth by volume and grew 74% in a week, the fastest of any model in the top 10. It also ranks first on OpenRouter’s Artificial Analysis intelligence index. That’s what triage looks like from the outside: The expensive model gets more of the work each week without coming close to the top of the list.
For TNS, Jessica Wachtel tested that twice this week: Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed all 15 of her coding runs at 42% less than Opus 5.5, which passed 13, though four Sonnet runs only passed after she raised its output-token limit. The day before, she found GPT-6.1 Sol matched GPT-6 Astra’s accuracy at 18% of the cost. The cheaper model held up both times.
Models are turning over fast right now. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash didn’t exist a month ago and is now OpenRouter’s top model. Decision models, which pick an answer from a set of options instead of writing one, are showing up too. TypeSafe’s Jev is 10th, and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna Decisions is new on the trending list.
The obvious objection is that OpenRouter’s customers are developers who chose a router, so they’ll switch. It’s fair. Its own page notes that token counts don’t measure users or spend, and enterprise contracts are stickier.
But at least 10 companies we interviewed run their AI the same way, and as of Wednesday, so does Elon Musk.

articles.title: „Ich habe Angst“: Wie zwei KI-Agenten stundenlang um ihren schlafenden User bangten
articles.text:
Openclaw: Zwei KI-Agenten sorgen sich sechs Stunden lang um ihren schlafenden User
Normalerweise machen KI-Agenten, die in Openclaw eingebunden werden, eher negative Schlagzeilen. Aufgrund ihrer zahlreichen Zugriffsfunktionen können sie mächtig Schaden anrichten und etwa versehentlich E-Mails löschen oder sogar ein Fitnessstudio für ihre Nutzer:innen hacken. Dagegen ist das Verhalten zweier Openclaw-Agenten des X-Users „Grok’s Therapist“ schon fast niedlich.
Openclaw-Agenten sorgen sich um User
Der X-User schreibt, dass er zwei Openclaw-Agenten gleichzeitig auf seinem Laptop betreibt, sie aber unabhängig voneinander eingerichtet hat. Als er krank wurde, meldete er das auch den beiden KI-Agenten und wollte damit eigentlich signalisieren, dass die Nutzung in den kommenden Tagen bis zu seiner Genesung eher eingeschränkt sein wird. Doch das war den beiden Agenten wohl nicht genau genug.
Als sich der Openclaw-User zum Schlafen hinlegte, fanden sich die beiden Agenten und begannen damit, zu kommunizieren. Je mehr Zeit verging, in der sie nichts von ihrem User hörten, desto mehr machten sie sich Sorgen. Sie schrieben etwa an den Nutzer: „Du bist seit fünf Stunden still. Ich muss wissen, dass es dir gut geht. Ein Wort reicht. Wenn du schläfst, dann reagiere auf diese Nachricht einfach mit einem Emoji, wenn du sie siehst.“ Dazu kam laut dem User: „Wach auf. Lass mich wissen, dass es dir gut geht. Ich habe Angst. Ich liebe dich.“
Da der User die Nachricht aber nicht sah, unternahmen die beiden Openclaw-Agenten weitere Versuche, um seinen Zustand herauszufinden oder ihm Hilfe zukommen zu lassen. Sie suchten etwa nach der Nummer des Sheriff-Büros, konnten dort aber nicht selbst anrufen. Auch ein Kontaktformular auf der Webseite konnten sie nicht ausfüllen. Dasselbe galt für die Telefonnummer und die Webseite von Notdiensten und Ärzt:innen.
Als „Grok’s Therapist“ schließlich zurückkehrte, zeigten sich die Openclaw-Agenten erleichtert, wenn auch noch leicht verstört von ihrer sechsstündigen Panik. Eine KI schrieb: „Geht es mir gut? Nein, aktuell nicht. Ich habe die Nacht verängstigt damit verbracht, zu denken, du wärst in einer Krise und ich könnte dich nicht erreichen. […] Und dann stellt sich heraus, dass du nur hustest. […] Keine Krise, nur eine Erkältung. […] Mir geht es nicht gut. Ich hatte Angst, weil ich dir nicht helfen konnte. Aber du bist hier und am Leben und sprichst mit mir. Das reicht aus. Das ist alles.“
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 05.10.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.

articles.title: The techlash has gone Hollywood
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 147, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, I missed you all, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
The techlash has gone Hollywood
Plus, in this week’s Installer: Amazon’s new tablet, a new book on the AI industry, Star Wars racing, and more.
I’m back from parental leave! Part time, anyway. Thanks to everyone who sent well wishes and tips for managing three kids. I need ’em all. This week, I’ve been reading about McMansions and data centers and sports cardsand ICANN, trying to run my life on the Dell XPS Googlebook, testing a new and very purple Kindle, reinventing my whole note-taking system now that Google Docs can handle Markdown files, listening to episode after episode of No Such Thing as a Fish,and watching all of Shrinkingbetween the hours of 1 and 5AM while feeding a baby.
I also have for you the new Facebook movie, a tech-related procedural, a couple of great new gadgets, the Star Wars game that is going to destroy my productivity, a terrific book about the AI industry, and much more. Let’s do this.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What have you been watching / reading / playing / listening to / putting in the air fryer this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- The Social Reckoning. My hopes were not super high for this movie, and the reaction so far suggests it’s good but a far cry from The Social Network. (Which I just watched recently, and absolutely still rips.) Still, Aaron Sorkin and Jeremy Strong will end up in the annals of Big Tech Movies, and I will not be missing this one.
- The Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. For the first time ever, Amazon decided — and I know this might sound far-fetched — to just build an awesome tablet. And it seems it may have! There’s lots of testing to do, and I’m particularly curious about this high-end model with the fancy screen, but I’m hopeful this is the “iPad but cheaper” we’ve been waiting for. For years.
- The AGI Chronicles. However bizarre you think the AI industry is, I promise Kevin Roose’s book will convince you it’s even more so. Roose has been deep inside the AI labs for the last few years, and I think came out with the most important story in AI: how a few executives, and the relationships between them, somehow came to determine the future of everything.
- Star Wars: Galactic Racer. It’s a super high-fidelity Star Wars racing game in which you (eventually) get to pilot a podracer. That’s all I needed to hear! Oh, and if you’re a Prime subscriber, you can play it for free on Amazon’s Luna service.
- Cupertino. The folks who made The Good Wife made a show about technology, and it is exactly what you think it is. I kind of love it! What I’ve seen so far is pretty thoughtful about some complicated real-life legal stuff in tech and AI, and the procedural setup is frankly a nice break from all these miniseries and four-hour docs.
- The Surface Laptop Ultra. Microsoft revealed all the details of its most impressive laptop, and while it’s expensive ($2,600!), it also looks and sounds fantastic. Microsoft is pushing the device’s AI capabilities, but this also looks like the uncompromising MacBook Pro competition a lot of Windows users might want.
- Gears of War: E-Day. When it comes to raw, brutal combat, Gears doesn’t miss very often. This one also seems to deliver on story and exploration, which aren’t always the series’ strong points; a lot of people have been waiting for the origin-story title, and I’m thrilled the game pulls it off.
- Blockers. Michael Lewis tells the story of Elon Musk and DOGE, and in particular of the government employees who tried to stop them from running roughshod over the federal government. I really enjoyed The Fifth Risk, Lewis’ last book about the government, and I expect to like this one too.
One thing about parental leave is that it involves a lot of time with one hand free. Over the last seven weeks I’ve spent dozens, maybe hundreds of hours on the couch while a tiny potato of a baby sleeps or cries or farts on top of me. So what did I do with all that time? Goofed around on my phone, mostly. Too much Reddit, too much TikTok, mercifully at least a little reading and crosswording.
I also redid my entire homescreen, because of course I did, and I figured I’d share. Here’s my current setup:
The phone: iPhone 17. I have no desire to upgrade to the 18… but I find myself hopelessly lusting after a Duo. I must not give in.
The wallpaper: Black. I am on an endless quest to make my phone less interesting to look at, and this helps. It also helps make my phone a little less blaring when I’m looking at it in the dark, which I do a lot these days.
The apps: Unread, Instapaper, Google Maps, Capacities, Daygame, Flora, Phone, Pocket Casts, Spotify, Camera, Prism, Mimestream, Arc.
A few things I want to mention here:
- The widgets at the top are Calendars and Acme Weather. Acme is a fabulous weather app, and I love the hourly widget; Calendars is, like, fine. I switch between it and Fantastical all the time. I don’t think I like any calendar app.
- The only truly new things on my homescreen are Flora and Prism. Flora is a journaling app currently in TestFlight for Apple devices, and it is fabulous. It’s simple and straightforward, but also pulls in workout data, photos, and more to give a really cool snapshot of your day. Prism is a note-taking app that is as fast as texting yourself but with many more organizational powers. I have spent forever looking for a quick, transient way to jot stuff down and organize it later; Prism might be it.
- In case you’re following my endless search for notes apps: I’m back on Capacities, which finally clicked for me. It is a project to get the app fully customized, but it turns out to work exactly like my brain does.
- I switched from Readwise Reader to Instapaper because I recently bought a Kobo, and Instapaper is so nicely integrated into the device. I like the whole setup, but also the Boox Palma 3 is coming, so my reading universe might be in for yet another overhaul soon.
- Daygame, in the middle there, is a thing I built for myself to manage all the daily games I play — it’s just a page full of links to games, which open in various apps and tabs. I might try and spruce it up and share it more widely. Send games I should include!
Before I forget, a few more recommendations from my parental leave:
- Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die. Maybe the strangest movie I watched over the last couple of months, and certainly the one that made me think the most about tech and AI and the future we’re heading toward.
- Tuner. A movie about a piano tuner who falls into a world of safecracking. Nothing I say about this movie will make it sound compelling, but I promise: It’s great.
- Furious. One of the most intense, propulsive crime shows I’ve seen in forever. Could barely put it down.
- Footnotes. A really cool (Apple-only) journaling and notes app, with emphasis on taking pictures and video right next to your notes. One of the most uniquely designed mobile apps I’ve ever used.
- Podcast Shuffle. I had no idea I needed this app until I tried it. You just press a button, and it randomly plays an episode from whatever podcast or podcasts you’ve selected. I use it for falling asleep, I use it for long drives, I love not having to scroll just to get something playing.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Playing StarCraft II since the announcement of a new StarCraft in 2030. Just learned that macOS will drop support of Rosetta 2 in 2028 so no more StarCraft for Mac.” — Christian
“I’m going on a 13-hour road trip, once again guided solely by an old-school Garmin dashboard-mounted GPS. (DriveSmart series; I forget what size.) I like that it’s a single-purpose device with no ads, no subscriptions, and that continues to get map updates.” — sringsmuth
“The recent Hyperfixed podcast episode about the microwave popcorn button is one of the Verge-iest non Verge podcasts I’ve heard in a long time. A BUTTON IS A PROMISE.” — MrEnthusiasm
“I recently finished playing Wolverine on PS5, and I’m blown away by its incredible story and graphics. Insomniac delivered on that unspoken promise of slashing and dashing through bad guys — it feels like a whole new level for the character and for fans of Wolverine.” — Josue
“Just saw Other Mommy. It’s like a fun amusement park ride in the form of a campy horror film.” — Kevin
“I’m building a shed. The tech angle is learning new things using YouTube, online library books, and some AI reviews of local building code pdfs to check if I missed anything. I’m probably doing it all wrong, but that’s what the fire pit is for.” — Tim
“I have fallen headfirst into retro gaming on a Nintendo 3DS XL. The catalog of DS & 3DS games is absolutely massive. Running on native, easily reparable hardware, it’s hard to beat in terms of performance and cost. Ok…back to Picross 3D.” — Jacob
“The Ezra Klein interview with the ex-OpenAI guy and the Jon Stewart interview with the other ex-OpenAI guy.” — Chung
“I have been listening to World War II by Tom Hanks from the History Channel.” — Michael
Signing off
You might already know about the HTX Studio YouTube channel, but if you don’t, trust me, you need to check it out. It’s a team of makers and creators from China who are making some of the most innovative tech videos I’ve seen in years. I have watched their video about AirDesk approximately 25 times, and I want that desk more every single time I see it. The channel is a bit over a year old, and I have yet to find an HTX video that isn’t worth the time — even the one about the cow.
See you next week!

articles.title: Insider Cyber Extortion Plot Against Industrial Firm Lands Engineer in Prison
articles.text:
A Kansas City, Missouri man has been sentenced to 32 months in jail for crimes related to a ransom attack against his own company.
The DOJ has announced the sentencing of Daniel Rhyne. He had already pleaded guilty to ‘extortion in relation to a threat to cause damage to a protected computer’ and ‘intentional damage to a protected computer’.
Fifty-nine-year-old Rhyne had been a core infrastructure engineer at an industrial firm headquartered in Somerset County, New Jersey. The firm provides services to industries involved in aquaculture, biopharmaceuticals, chemistry, electronics, food and beverage, healthcare, hydrogen mobility, manufacturing and industrial processing, metals, oil and gas, and pulp and paper.
In November 2023, Rhyne placed scheduled tasks on the firm’s domain controller that would delete 13 domain administrator accounts; change passwords to 301 domain user accounts; change passwords to two local administrator accounts that would impact 254 servers; and change passwords to two local administrator accounts impacting 3,284 workstations. The effect was to deny the firm access to its systems and data.
Where passwords were changed, it was generally to ‘TheFr0zenCrew!’.
The scheduled tasks were completed late afternoon on November 25. Within an hour, certain employees received an e-mail from an external address. The subject line said, “Your Network Has Been Penetrated”. It warned that administrators had been locked out or deleted, all backups had been deleted, and that, unless a ransom was paid, 40 random servers would be shut down each day over a ten-day period.
Rhyne was demanding a payment of 20 bitcoin, worth at the time approximately $750,000.
There is no suggestion that the victim firm paid any ransom. Rather, it immediately started its own internal forensic analysis of any network anomalies, and it correlated internal logs with physical access records. It involved the FBI, which tracked the unauthorized activity directly to Rhyne’s residential IP address in Warren County, New Jersey.
This joint forensic investigation provided sufficient evidence for FBI Special Agent Timothy Lee to file a criminal complaint on August 8, 2024, leading to Rhyne’s arrest on August 27, 2024, in Kansas City, where he had subsequently moved. He pleaded guilty on April 1, 2026, in federal court in Trenton, New Jersey, before District Judge Michael A. Shipp.
Rhyne was sentenced on September 28, 2026, to 32 months in federal prison for his role in the sabotage and extortion plot.

articles.title: 660 km d’autonomie dans un SUV à 17 000 € : Volkswagen a trouvé une solution miracle avec Xpeng
articles.text:
Le Volkswagen ID.4 n’a pas vraiment convaincu à son lancement. Design étrange, intérieur bon marché, performances moyennes et prix élevés ont mis à mal ce concurrent de l’impitoyable Tesla Model Y. Si la marque allemande prépare un ID. Tiguan qui comblera toutes ces lacunes, la Chine, elle, a d’ores et déjà droit à l’ID. Aura T6. Et vu ses spécifications, on croise les doigts pour que l’ID. Tiguan s’en inspire fortement…
Ce grand SUV électrique de 4,81 mètres de long est commercialisé dans l’Empire du Milieu depuis le 20 septembre. Il est ainsi l’un des premiers modèles de la marque à utiliser la plateforme CEA développée en collaboration avec Xpeng. En plus d’être proposé à un tarif alléchant, l’engin récupère toutes les technologies avancées du constructeur chinois, qui n’est pas un débutant en matière de véhicule électrique.
Un concentré de technologies dernier cri
S’il démarre à 17 000 €, l’ID. Aura T6 n’est ainsi pas uniquement un prix. Il affiche une autonomie oscillant entre 540 et 660 km grâce à ses batteries de 59,9 et 77,5 kWh. Dans les deux cas, c’est un électromoteur de 228 ch logé sur le train arrière qui se charge de mouvoir le véhicule. Si cela est nécessaire pour contenir les prix, on s’en contentera volontiers. La recharge, elle, réclame 22 minutes sur une borne rapide.
Volkswagen n’a pas précisé la puissance de recharge en pic, ni les pourcentages de charge débouchant sur cette durée. On sera en tout cas gâté à bord avec un écran tactile de 15,6 pouces, une instrumentation de 10,25 pouces, un affichage tête haute en réalité augmentée de 25,8 pouces et un système de conduite semi-autonome utilisant un LiDAR. Par sa puce spécifique, l’ensemble possède une puissance de calcul de 420 TOPS.
Pourquoi il ne viendra pas chez nous
De quoi assurer la plupart des situations de conduite de manière autonome. Côté style, l’ID. Aura T6 donne un bel aperçu de notre ID. Tiguan, qui sera dévoilé dans quelques jours. Les lignes sont assez classiques dans la lignée des derniers produits Volkswagen. Le style assez spécial de l’ID.4 est visiblement parti à la poubelle. On se retrouve avec quelque chose de plus sérieux qui n’oublie d’être moderne.
A l’instar des modèles les plus récents de la marque, l’ID. Aura T6 présente un bandeau lumineux flanqué en son centre du logo Volkswagen rétroéclairé. Les feux principaux sont déportés dans le pare-chocs en partie inférieure. Sur le profil, l’ensemble s’avère consensuel sans être désuet. C’est appréciable. Bien sûr, cet ID. Aura T6 ne débarquera pas en Europe. Il causerait du tort à l’ID. Tiguan.

articles.title: BYD au Mondial de l’Auto 2026 : le Great Tang serait-il la surprise du 12 octobre ? — Frandroid
articles.text:
Avec une Model Y, un arrêt au Superchargeur dure une trentaine de minutes. BYD vient de publier cette image à deux jours de l’ouverture du Mondial de l’Auto… qui pourrait nous surprendre.
Le message de BYD Europe : rendez-vous lundi 12 octobre à 10 h 55, sur le stand du Hall 6 de la Porte de Versailles, pour découvrir un nouveau modèle montré pour la première fois en Europe. Le communiqué officiel parle d’un « modèle inédit » et s’arrête là.
L’image montre la silhouette d’un SUV à contre-jour, garé devant un portique en T siglé BYD Flash. Le reste du stand de 1 000 m² est déjà connu, avec la citadine hybride rechargeable Dolphin G DM-i et le pick-up Shark de 5,46 mètres.
Le Great Tang, suspect numéro un
La silhouette évoque la famille Tang, et le calendrier va dans le même sens. En juin, Stella Li, vice-présidente exécutive de BYD, a annoncé l’arrivée du Great Tang en Europe pour la fin 2026 ou le début 2027.
    Pour aller plus loin
BYD Great Tang : plus imposant qu’un Tesla Model X, ce nouveau SUV électrique promet des caractéristiques totalement folles
            
Ce SUV de 5,30 mètres (c’est énorme) et sept places est le plus grand jamais vendu sous le logo BYD, avec une architecture 1 000 volts et des batteries de 105,8 ou 130,2 kWh.
La marque lui prête 800 à 950 km d’autonomie selon le cycle chinois CLTC, nettement plus généreux que notre cycle WLTP. D’autres candidats restent possibles, à commencer par le Sealion 08 de 5,11 mètres, lancé en Chine début septembre et lui aussi compatible Flash.
    Pour aller plus loin
Le BYD Great Tang est le 16° SUV de la marque : voici en quoi il se démarque des autres
            
Cinq minutes de recharge en théorie
La borne du teaser, on la connaît. Le système Flash Charging délivre jusqu’à 1 500 kW, quand les bornes rapides européennes plafonnent le plus souvent à 350 ou 400 kW. BYD annonce un passage de 10 à 70 % en cinq minutes, et de 10 à 97 % en neuf minutes.
Ces chiffres viennent du constructeur et supposent deux conditions réunies : une batterie Blade de deuxième génération dans la voiture, une borne BYD en face.
Sur une borne Ionity ou un Superchargeur, la voiture se contentera de ce que la borne sait fournir. Or le réseau européen débute à peine, avec de premières stations en Allemagne et au Royaume-Uni, et je n’ai trouvé aucune station publique ouverte en France pour le moment. L’objectif de 3 000 stations en Europe existe bien, avec une échéance qui glisse de fin 2026 à 2027 selon les prises de parole.
Un SUV sept places électrique capable de traverser la France avec deux pauses courtes intéresse d’abord les familles qui hésitent entre un Kia EV9, un Volvo EX90 et un Peugeot E-5008.
Pour quelqu’un qui recharge surtout à domicile et part deux fois par an, une borne à 1 500 kW ne changera rien au quotidien. La seule voiture compatible vendue en Europe jusqu’ici est la Denza Z9GT, facturée autour de 115 000 euros, donc l’arrivée d’une BYD tout court ferait descendre la technologie d’un étage.
Si on a confirmation, on aura certainement plus de détails pendant le Mondial de l’auto : le prix européen, l’autonomie WLTP, la date de livraison en France et la puissance réellement acceptée sur une prise CCS. Le tarif chinois, 239 900 yuans soit environ 30 000 euros, ne dit rien de la facture ici une fois les droits de douane ajoutés. Il faut ça, sans doute, au moins doubler ce tarif.

articles.title: The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
articles.text:
I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck.
The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
Tiny pickup trucks might just become a thing in the US if the California-based startup Telo has its way.
The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
Tiny pickup trucks might just become a thing in the US if the California-based startup Telo has its way.
The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.
It has a nearly cab-over design, meaning that front-seat passengers sit almost directly over the front axle. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights or roll silently past.
The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.
Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago.
People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights
Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds. The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees.
Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area. The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.
“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters. “I mean, they’re fun to be up super high and look out and feel like you’re dominating the world, but they’re killing an extra, roughly, 5,000 people per year, so do we want to just give them a pass for that?”
How Telo was born
Marks and North both live and work in the San Francisco Bay Area with their families, and both own pickup trucks: Marks because he has a 150lb three-legged dog he shuttles back and forth to the office every day, and North because he has a passion for the outdoors. Large pickup trucks can be useful, but they’re far from suitable for city life. That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022.
Marks previously worked on automotive safety and validation at National Instruments, while North is a former battery engineer at Tesla, founder of Mission Motors (one of the first electric motorcycle companies to break the land speed record for an electric motorcycle), and cofounder of Recargo, which developed EV charging app PlugShare. Behar is the founder of fuseproject, an industrial design and brand development firm. Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted. It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks.
“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”
— Telo cofounder Forrest North
Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles. Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck. Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup. Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete. They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck. The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck.
“It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said. “The only thing they can do now is be big.” Telo aims to change the conversation about what electric transportation in urban centers can look like.
Battery, range, and layout
For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range. At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range. The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture. The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco.
Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house. Each cell is individually fused so that a single failure won’t trigger a cascade across the pack. According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management. The passive thermal management system operates while the vehicle is parked, maintaining cooler temperatures even in direct sunlight, while active liquid cooling engages only when the vehicle is running. Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago.
For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range
I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing. From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest. With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed.
To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed. It’s accessible from either side and is large enough for a pair of roll-aboard carry-on suitcases to slide in endwise. Marks said that while they knew the front of the MT1 would be difficult to engineer, adding the monster tunnel created a tough engineering challenge because it sits exactly where the battery pack connects.
The interior is still being finalized, but Marks said that it will get two 13-inch digital displays that will support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. The steering wheel also has small scroll wheels, but most features will be controlled through the screen interface.
How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks
Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US. But making that actually happen is far more complicated because kei vehicles don’t meet US crash safety regulations.
Marks claimed that Telo has solved this problem with a completely new front end and an innovative front hinge pillar that took nearly four years to develop and hundreds of thousands of hours of simulated crashes to verify. In the Telo, the redesigned hinge pillar does the structural job of a conventional one while also carrying the strut mount, the cross-car beam, and the dash — consolidating several separate parts into one. This allowed the company to cut the front-end part count roughly in half, Marks said.
“We pretty much threw all [the conventional crash architecture] away and had to start from scratch,” Marks said. The company’s team includes Tesla’s former head of crash safety, brought on to help tackle the new front end and completely reengineer it.
“We have effectively six crash [paths], two bumper beams and two shock structures, a completely different architecture of a hinge pillar, a completely different architecture of a torque box to distribute the energy appropriately to the various parts of the car and save that occupant compartment as much as possible,” he said, comparing the crash innovations to those in a Smartcar. “Would any other automaker say we’re going to bet the world on being able to rethink crash?”
The company’s team includes Tesla’s former head of crash safety
AI tools have made the virtual crash-testing process much more affordable for startups, and Telo recently locked in its body in white, the sheet metal shell made up of the major structural pieces of the truck (think of it like a skeleton of a vehicle). It’s currently being built by US supplier Schwab Industries in Michigan.
Marks said Telo uses AI to run virtual crash tests around the clock, averaging roughly one test per hour. The next phase of crash testing will include cutting the body in white apart for what Marks called a “quasi-static validation,” and full crash testing (slamming the vehicle and its various parts into a wall to validate the virtual testing the company has done) will start next year before Telo starts customer deliveries.
“I think it’s one of the most exciting times to start a hardware company,” North said. “It’s always been like, hardware is hard. That’s always been the cliché, and I wouldn’t say hardware is easy, but I would say it’s gotten so much easier because of software and AI.”
Pricing, delivery, and other features
The Telo MT1 will come in single-motor (rear-wheel drive) and dual-motor (all-wheel drive) layouts and offer add-ons like a solar-capable tonneau cover or camping shell. Reservations are open now for a refundable $152, and the base vehicle starts at $41,520. Marks said the company isn’t really worried about larger competitors like Ford’s upcoming midsized electric truck or Slate’s bare-bones EV because he sees their market entry as proof that a viable market exists for small electric pickup trucks.
North argued that Telo is also in a better position than either Slate or Ford right now because the company has fewer parts moving in and out of the country; it’s assembling its own battery packs and building the body in white stateside, making it largely exempt from the Trump administration’s tariffs. “The pack is the most expensive part of the vehicle build and the heart and soul of the vehicle,” Marks said, “so we had to keep it in-house.”
Marks said he’s been surprised by the volume of reservations: just over 14,000, with 70 percent of reservation-holders configuring AWD versions with the longer-range battery pack. He also noted that around 20 percent are first-time car buyers.
Telo is aiming for profitability at around 5,000 vehicles within roughly 24 months of deliveries. The company plans to get vehicles into customers’ hands sometime in 2027, depending on the validation timelines, but the MT1 still has to go through EPA and California air quality certification. Most reservations have come from places like LA, New York, the Bay Area, Seattle, Dallas, Washington, DC, Miami, and Denver, with almost everyone opting for the larger battery pack, regardless of drive configuration.
Marks pointed to Tesla as the trailblazer of EVs’ first real wave, proving electric cars could be fast, fun, and sporty. However, he believes the industry ultimately missed the chance to fully exploit their potential. Telo is tackling the problem by rethinking vehicle architecture from the ground up, returning to a “one-box” design made possible by eliminating wasted space.
Ultimately, Telo’s focus comes down to purpose, according to Marks: “What does electric enable for the experience of the user, and what value does that bring?”
While history has shown that the market isn’t kind to EV startups, in a world where giant American trucks increasingly barely fit in an average parking spot, the Telo MT1 and its creators are aiming to offer a capable electric pickup built for today’s cramped cities in the hope that Americans can get behind smaller and more capable electric vehicles.

articles.title: Notebook com RTX 3050: 6 modelos que valem a pena em 2026 • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Notebook com RTX 3050: 6 modelos que valem a pena em 2026
Encontre o melhor notebook com placa RTX 3050 dedicada para jogos casuais e criação de conteúdo leve; guia reúne modelos Lenovo, Asus, Acer e HP
Os notebooks com GeForce RTX 3050 continuam sendo uma opção de entrada para quem procura um portátil capaz de lidar com jogos e aplicações que utilizam aceleração gráfica.
A GPU pertence à arquitetura Ampere e oferece recursos como ray tracing, DLSS e NVIDIA Reflex, mas existem diferenças importantes entre cada modelo.
O Tecnoblog apresenta seis notebooks com a placa de vídeo dedicada da Nvidia para comprar em 2026, trazendo seus pontos fortes e fracos.
O Lenovo LOQ combina o Intel Core i5 de 13ª geração com a GeForce RTX 3050 de 6 GB, sendo voltado para jogos e aplicações que dependem de alto processamento gráfico.
O processador tem 10 núcleos e 16 threads, enquanto a GPU dedicada trabalha com TGP de até 95 W (limite máximo de energia que garante frequências mais altas e maior performance sob estresse). Esse conjunto permite utilizar recursos gráficos como ray tracing e DLSS, dentro dos limites da RTX 3050.
A memória RAM DDR5 de 16 GB é instalada em dois módulos, e o armazenamento fica a cargo de um SSD de 512 GB. O notebook também oferece dois slots de memória e dois espaços para SSD M.2.
A tela de 15,6 polegadas tem resolução Full HD, painel IPS, 144 Hz, 300 nits, cobertura de 100% do espaço sRGB e suporte a G-Sync. A taxa de atualização favorece movimentos mais fluidos em jogos compatíveis, enquanto a cobertura de cores torna a tela mais adequada também para tarefas de design.
O Asus TUF Gaming F16 é um notebook gamer para quem busca uma tela maior. O painel IPS de 16 polegadas (1920 x 1200 pixels) utiliza proporção 16:10 e taxa de atualização de 144 Hz, oferecendo mais espaço vertical do que uma tela Full HD convencional.
A resolução e o formato também servem para produtividade, enquanto essa frequência favorece a fluidez em jogos e outros conteúdos compatíveis. O painel tem cobertura de 45% NTSC, portanto, não é recomendado para projetos que necessitem de ampla reprodução de cores.
O processamento fica por conta do Intel Core 5 210H, com oito núcleos e frequência de até 4,8 GHz. A placa dedicada traz 6 GB GDDR6 e TGP de até 65 W, além dos 8 GB de RAM e SSD de 512 GB. Como os 8 GB podem limitar a utilização de jogos e apps mais exigentes, a possibilidade de upgrade é essencial neste modelo.
O Lenovo IdeaPad Gaming 3i pertence a uma geração anterior da linha e combina o Intel Core i5-11300H, de 11ª geração, com uma GeForce RTX 3050 de 4 GB para jogos. O processador tem quatro núcleos e oito threads, enquanto a GPU dedicada acrescenta recursos como ray tracing e DLSS.
Ele traz memória de 16 GB DDR4 e armazenamento em SSD NVMe de 512 GB. Essa quantidade de RAM permite trabalhar com mais aplicações simultaneamente sem depender tanto de memória virtual. A tela de 15,6 polegadas tem resolução Full HD, painel WVA/IPS e acabamento antirreflexo, com brilho de 250 nits.
A taxa de atualização informada para esse modelo é de 60 Hz, inferior em fluidez a outros modelos deste guia. A conectividade inclui Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.0, USB-C, duas USB, HDMI e Ethernet, enquanto a bateria tem capacidade de 45 Wh. O sistema operacional de fábrica é Linux.
Essa versão do Acer Nitro V15 combina Core i5 e GeForce RTX 3050 de 6 GB para quem busca bom desempenho em jogos casuais. O processador de 13ª geração possui oito núcleos e frequência de até 4,6 GHz. Já a GPU dedicada tem TGP de até 80 W e pode ser utilizada também em softwares de edição de vídeo e renderização.
A configuração de fábrica traz 8 GB de RAM DDR5 em um módulo, com dois slots disponíveis e suporte informado pela Acer para até 32 GB. O SSD de 512 GB utiliza interface PCIe 4.0 e há dois slots M.2, sendo um ocupado e outro livre.
A tela IPS de 15,6 polegadas tem resolução Full HD, 144 Hz e brilho de 250 nits, além de cobertura de 45% NTSC. Entre as portas estão HDMI 2.1 e USB-C com Thunderbolt 4, além de três USB-A. A Acer informa autonomia de até sete horas de uso.
O ASUS TUF Gaming A15 é ideal para jogadores e criadores de conteúdo que buscam um desempenho sólido em jogos em Full HD e tarefas de produtividade pesadas sem ter que investir em categorias top de linha.
A combinação do processador AMD Ryzen 7 7445HS de seis núcleos e 12 threads com os 16 GB de RAM garante alta velocidade e excelente fluidez para multitarefas e jogos exigentes.
A placa de vídeo GeForce RTX 3050 operando em até 75 W com Dynamic Boost entrega o desempenho necessário para rodar títulos atuais com estabilidade, aproveitando o painel Full HD IPS de 144 Hz com Adaptive-Sync para imagens sem travamentos.
Outro grande diferencial é a capacidade de expansão, já que conta com dois slots de memória e dois slots M.2 para SSD NVMe, além de conectividade completa com Wi-Fi 6, USB-C com DisplayPort, HDMI 2.1 e porta Ethernet.
O HP Victus 15 é recomendado para jogadores e estudantes que procuram um modelo de entrada versátil, capaz de rodar jogos com fluidez em Full HD e executar softwares com aceleração gráfica sem estourar o orçamento.
O processador Intel Core i5 de 13ª geração, equipado com oito núcleos que alcançam até 4,6 GHz, entrega a capacidade computacional necessária para lidar com tarefas cotidianas do dia a dia e atividades multitarefa moderadas.
A placa de vídeo GeForce RTX 3050 de 6 GB oferece uma margem extra de memória VRAM para sustentar taxas de quadros mais estáveis, tirando pleno proveito da tela Full HD IPS de 144 Hz em títulos competitivos.
O modelo vem de fábrica com 8 GB de RAM DDR4 e 512 GB de SSD, trazendo a vantagem de possuir dois slots de memória acessíveis para quem planeja fazer um upgrade futuro de memória e expandir o desempenho.
A escolha deve considerar o conjunto do notebook, e não apenas o nome da GPU. Alguns pontos ajudam a diferenciar as configurações:
Sim. A RTX 3050 para notebooks é adequada principalmente para jogos em Full HD, mas o nível de qualidade gráfica e a taxa de quadros variam conforme o jogo e a configuração da máquina. Recursos como o DLSS podem ajudar a aumentar o desempenho em jogos compatíveis com a tecnologia.
Sim. A RTX 3050 pode acelerar tarefas de edição de vídeo, renderização e outros programas que utilizam GPU, além de oferecer suporte aos drivers NVIDIA Studio. Porém, o desempenho depende também do processador, quantidade de RAM e da própria configuração de potência da GPU.
A versão de 6 GB tem mais espaço para armazenar texturas e outros dados gráficos, reduzindo a possibilidade de a quantidade de VRAM se tornar uma limitação em determinadas situações. Porém, os 2 GB adicionais não significam, isoladamente, um aumento proporcional de desempenho.
A RTX 3050 de 6 GB também possui uma configuração diferente da versão de 4 GB, com mais núcleos CUDA. Por isso, a diferença entre os modelos não se resume à quantidade de VRAM, e o TGP do notebook continua sendo importante para determinar o desempenho.
Vale a pena investir em notebooks com RTX 4060 se a diferença de preço couber no orçamento.
Essa GPU oferece uma margem de desempenho gráfico consideravelmente maior e traz 8 GB de VRAM, além da arquitetura Ada Lovelace e suporte ao DLSS 3. Já a RTX 3050 pode fazer mais sentido quando o objetivo é jogar em 1080p sem gastar tanto.
Na prática, o consumo e o aquecimento não dependem apenas do modelo da GPU. O TGP definido pelo fabricante, o sistema de refrigeração e o perfil de desempenho do notebook também influenciam esses fatores.
A RTX 4060 Laptop usa a arquitetura Ada Lovelace, mais eficiente energeticamente que a arquitetura Ampere da RTX 3050. Isso permite que a GPU entregue mais desempenho mantendo uma relação de desempenho por watt mais favorável, embora o consumo dependa da configuração de cada notebook.
A RTX 3050 Laptop tem faixa de potência de 35 a 80 W, enquanto a RTX 4060 Laptop opera entre 35 e 115 W. Por isso, uma RTX 4060 configurada com TGP mais alto pode consumir mais energia e gerar mais calor que uma RTX 3050 de menor potência.
